T_C01_S01_INTRO1::block-0: Salutation 1. Salutation to Him, the Self whose very nature is Knowledge — from whom this entire universe is born, in whom alone it dissolves at the time of pralaya, and by whom indeed it is sustained throughout its continuance. To that Self, who is pure Consciousness and the one ground of origination, sustenance and dissolution, I bow.
T_C01_S01_INTRO1::block-1: Salutation 2. To those teachers (gurus) by whom, in former times, all the Vedānta texts were expounded with full mastery — through the analysis of words (pada), sentences (vākya), and the means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa) — to them I am ever and constantly bowed down in reverence.
T_C01_S01_INTRO1::block-2: Salutation 3. Of the Taittirīyaka — that is, of the essence of the Taittirīya recension of the Veda — by the grace of the ācārya (the preceptor's lineage), this commentary is now being composed by me, for the sake of those whose taste is set on a clearly stated meaning (vispaṣṭa-artha-rucīnām).
T_C01_S01_INTRO1::block-3:
Introductory bhāṣya. In the earlier portion of the text (the Karma-kāṇḍa, and within the Āraṇyaka the previous chapters dealing with rites), the obligatory rites (nitya-karmāṇi) — meant for the destruction of the demerit accumulated through past actions — and the optional desire-prompted rites (kāmya-karmāṇi) — for those who long for specific results — have been already set forth. Now, for the sake of removing the very cause that drives one to take up further karma, the knowledge of Brahman (brahma-vidyā) is here begun.

The cause of karma is desire (kāma), since it is desire that impels one to act. For those whose desires are already fulfilled (āpta-kāma), there can be no engagement in action, since, in the absence of desire, they remain established in their own Self; and where there is no impulsion, no activity arises. And being established in the Self is itself the state of fulfilled desire (āpta-kāmatā), for the Self is Brahman. The śruti will indeed declare that the knower of Brahman attains the Supreme. Therefore, when avidyā has been removed, abiding in one's own Self is itself the attainment of the Supreme — as the śruti says, ‘He attains the fearless Foundation' (Tai. Up. 2.7.1) and ‘He enters into this Self that is ānandamaya' (Tai. Up. 2.8.5).

For one possessed of knowledge, mokṣa arises as it were spontaneously (ayatnataḥ), without any further effort: the kāmya rites and the prohibited acts are not undertaken (since their motivating desire is gone); the karma already fructified (ārabdha) is exhausted by being lived through; and through the performance of the obligatory nityas there is no demerit (pratyavāya). Hence, abiding in one's own Self is mokṣa.

Objection (pūrvapakṣa): Why, then, accept knowledge at all? Surely mokṣa can arise from karma alone — for the surpassing happiness (niratiśayā prīti) which is denoted by the word ‘svarga' is itself produced by karma; therefore mokṣa too, being only a higher form of such happiness, may simply be brought about by karma.

Reply (siddhānta): No, that cannot be. Karma is manifold. There are countless deeds — some whose fruit has already begun (ārabdha-phala), and many more whose fruit has not yet begun (anārabdha-phala) — accumulated over numerous past births and yielding mutually opposed fruits. Of these, the unbegun ones cannot possibly be exhausted by enjoyment within a single life; therefore the residual karma must give rise to further bodies. The existence of such residual karma is established by hundreds of śruti and smṛti texts, such as ‘Now those whose conduct here has been pleasant…' (Chā. Up. 5.10.7) and ‘Then with the residue…' (Āp. Dh. 2.2.2.3; Gau. Smṛ. 11).

Objection: Then let the obligatory nitya rites be precisely for the exhaustion of the unbegun karmas, both desirable and undesirable in fruit.

Reply: No, since the śruti speaks of pratyavāya (demerit, evil) as resulting from their omission. The very word pratyavāya signifies an undesirable result. The nityas are accepted as serving to ward off a future suffering — namely the pratyavāya which would arise if they were not performed — and not as means of destroying unbegun-fruit karma. Even if for argument's sake we admitted that the nityas destroy unbegun-fruit karma, they could only consume the impure (aśuddha); they could not consume the pure, since there can be no opposition between two things of the same nature. Karma yielding desirable fruit is of pure character, and there is no possible contradiction between such pure karma and the nityas. Opposition is reasonable only between the pure and the impure.

Nor again can it be said that, since desires (the cause of karma) cannot cease in the absence of knowledge, the total destruction of karma is anyway impossible without vidyā — for desire belongs only to the non-knower of the Self, since its objects are non-Self results. In one's own Self there can be no desire, since the Self is eternally already attained; and the Self has been declared to be Para Brahman.

Further, the non-performance of the nityas is a mere absence (abhāva); from a mere absence no positive effect (such as pratyavāya) can possibly arise. Hence, the pratyavāya which the śruti speaks of must be understood as the unfolding of evil consequences from previously accumulated demerit (pūrva-upacita-durita), where the omission of the nitya is only the occasion (lakṣaṇa) — the absence of the obstruction that the nityas would have provided. Thus the participial form of ‘akurvan vihitaṁ karma' (Manu 11.44) — ‘he who, while not performing the prescribed rite (suffers thereby)' — is grammatically and metaphysically intelligible: the suffering arises from prior demerit, the non-performance merely allowing it to manifest. To suppose otherwise — that something positive springs from sheer non-existence — would overturn every pramāṇa.

Therefore, the position that ‘abiding in the Self arises spontaneously through karma' is untenable. As to the further claim that the supreme happiness called svarga, being produced by karma, supports the view that mokṣa too is initiated by karma — that also fails, because mokṣa is eternal (nitya). Nothing eternal is initiated; in worldly experience, whatever is initiated is non-eternal. Hence mokṣa cannot be brought about by karma.

Objection: Karmas accompanied by knowledge (vidyā-sahita) might have the power to initiate the eternal mokṣa.

Reply: No, this is self-contradictory. ‘Eternal' and ‘initiated' cannot stand together.

Objection: As pradhvaṁsābhāva (the cessation of a thing) is itself eternal, yet it is brought about (when the thing perishes), so mokṣa, though eternal, may be initiated.

Reply: No; for mokṣa is of the nature of being (bhāva-rūpa) — it is the eternally established Self itself — and is not a mere absence comparable to the cessation following destruction. (The argument continues; the bhāṣya here passes on to refute further alternatives and to establish that mokṣa, identical with the ever-existent Self, can be obtained only through vidyā.)
T_C01_S01_V01: Om. May Mitra grant us well-being; may Varuṇa grant us well-being; may Aryaman grant us well-being; may Indra and Bṛhaspati grant us well-being; may Viṣṇu of wide strides grant us well-being. Salutation to Brahman. Salutation to thee, O Vāyu! Thou indeed art the perceptible Brahman. Thee alone shall I declare to be the perceptible Brahman. I shall declare the right (ṛta); I shall declare the true (satya). May That protect me; may That protect the speaker. May It protect me; may It protect the speaker. Om. Peace, peace, peace.
T_C01_S01_V01::block-0:
‘Śam' means happiness, the absence of obstruction. May Mitra — the deity who is the abhimāni (presiding intelligence) of the prāṇa-vṛtti and of the day — be ‘śam', a giver of well-being, ‘naḥ', to us. Likewise, may Varuṇa, the presiding deity of the apāna-vṛtti and of the night, be a giver of well-being to us; Aryaman, the deity who presides over the eye and the sun; Indra, who presides over strength; Bṛhaspati, who presides over speech and the intellect (buddhi); and Viṣṇu, the uru-krama, ‘the wide-strider' (vistīrṇa-krama), who presides over the feet — these and similar adhyātma-deities (presiding over the bodily functions). The phrase ‘śam no bhavatu' is to be supplied with each one.

When these deities are gracious, the listening to vidyā, its retention, and its application proceed without impediment; therefore the seeker prays for their bestowal of well-being — ‘śam no bhavatu', ‘may it be well with us'. The aspirant for the knowledge of Brahman performs the actions of obeisance (namaskāra) and the declaration of Brahman (brahma-vadana) directed toward Vāyu, in order that any obstacle to the rise of brahma-vidyā may be pacified — for the fruits of all actions depend upon Him.

Vāyu is here regarded as Brahman; hence ‘namo brahmaṇe' — ‘to that Brahman I bend down (prahvī-bhāvaṁ karomi)' — the verb ‘I make' is to be supplied. ‘Namaste' — ‘O Vāyu, salutation be to thee' — speaking now in the second person; thus by the indirect (parokṣa) and the direct (pratyakṣa) modes one and the same Vāyu is addressed.

Further: since thou alone, in comparison with the eye and the other organs, art the most external and yet most immediate (sannikṛṣṭa, avyavahita), thou art the ‘pratyakṣaṁ brahma' — the directly cognisable Brahman. Therefore I shall declare thee alone to be the perceptible Brahman. I shall speak ṛta — that which, in accord with śāstra and duty, has been firmly ascertained in the buddhi — and since that very ascertainment depends upon thee, I shall declare thee alone (as ṛta). I shall speak satya — that same ṛta when accomplished through speech and body; and since the body and speech too depend on thee for their functioning, it is thee alone whom I declare as satya. (Etymological note (nirvacana): ṛta is the truth as held in the intellect; satya is that same truth as carried into expression and action.)

May that universal Brahman, here named Vāyu, being thus praised by me, protect me, the seeker of vidyā, by joining me with the knowledge; and may that very Brahman protect the speaker — the ācārya — by joining him with the capacity to expound. The repetition ‘avatu mām, avatu vaktāram' is for emphasis (ādara-artham). The threefold utterance ‘śāntiḥ śāntiḥ śāntiḥ' is for the pacification of the three classes of obstacles to the attainment of vidyā — the ādhyātmika (arising in oneself), the ādhibhautika (from other beings), and the ādhidaivika (from divine agencies).
T_C01_S02_V01: ‘We shall expound śīkṣā: letter, accent; quantity, effort; evenness, continuity. Thus has been told the chapter on śīkṣā.'
T_C01_S02_V01::block-0: Leading bhāṣya. Since the Upaniṣad's foremost concern is with the knowledge of meaning, lest the effort directed toward the correct recitation (grantha-pāṭha) be slackened, the chapter on śīkṣā is begun.
T_C01_S02_V01::block-1:
Etymology (nirvacana). ‘Śikṣā' — that by which (anayā) the letters and the rest are taught (śikṣyate); or, that in which (asmin) the letters and the rest are taught (śikṣyante) — namely the science treating of the utterance of varṇas and so forth. Thus śikṣā itself is śīkṣā; the lengthening of the i is a chāndasa (Vedic) usage.

‘Tāṁ śīkṣāṁ vyākhyāsyāmaḥ' — that very śīkṣā we shall expound, vispaṣṭam — clearly, ā samantāt — fully on every side, prakathayiṣyāmaḥ — we shall set forth. The form ‘vyākhyāsyāmaḥ' is from the root cakṣiṅ, replaced by khyāñ (by the rule cakṣiṅaḥ khyāñ-ādiṣṭasya), preceded by vi-āṅ, signifying ‘the act of speaking out distinctly' (vyakta-vāk-karman).

Within śīkṣā: varṇa is the letter — a, etc. svara is the accent — udātta and the rest. mātrā is quantity — short (hrasva) and the rest. balam is the special exertion or effort (prayatna-viśeṣa) of articulation. sāma is the evenness (samatā) of utterance, the middle pace (madhyama-vṛttyā uccāraṇam), neither too quick nor too slow. santāna is continuous junction, namely saṁhitā — the sandhi-joining of words.

Thus, the matter to be learned (śikṣitavyo'rthaḥ) is the ‘śīkṣā' here intended; the chapter (adhyāya) in which this is taught is the śīkṣādhyāya. ‘Iti uktaḥ' — ‘thus has it been declared'; the word ‘uktaḥ' is for upasaṁhāra, the concluding indication.
T_C01_S03_V01: ‘Be there glory together upon us both; be there spiritual lustre (brahma-varcas) together upon us both. Now, after this, we shall expound the upaniṣad of the saṁhitā (the joining of letters) under five headings — adhiloka (with reference to the worlds), adhijyotiṣa (with reference to luminaries), adhividya (with reference to learning), adhipraja (with reference to progeny), and adhyātma (with reference to the body). These they call the mahā-saṁhitās — ‘the great unions'. Now adhiloka: the earth is the prior form (pūrva-rūpa); the heaven, the latter form (uttara-rūpa); the sky (ākāśa) is the junction (sandhi).'
T_C01_S03_V01::block-0:
Now the upaniṣad of the saṁhitā is being taught. There, the yaśas — the renown — that is gained by knowing the upaniṣad on saṁhitā and so forth, ‘nau' — for us both, the disciple and the ācārya, ‘saha' — together — let it be. Likewise, may the brahma-varcas, the spiritual lustre arising from such knowledge, also be ours together. This is the prayer (āśīḥ) of the disciple. For prayer is appropriate to the disciple, who has not yet attained his end; not to the ācārya, who is already kṛta-artha (one whose work is accomplished) — for that is precisely what the word ‘ācārya' implies.

‘Atha' — now, after the foregoing — meaning after the rule for adhyayana (study by recitation) has been laid down. ‘Ataḥ' — therefore: because the intellect, having become extremely engrossed in the text (grantha-bhāvitā buddhiḥ), cannot suddenly be brought down upon the meaning, we shall expound the upaniṣad — the dṛśana, the contemplative vision — of saṁhitā, that is, having saṁhitā as its object, while the saṁhitā-text is still close at hand (grantha-sannikṛṣṭa). This is set forth in five adhikaraṇas — five āśrayas, supports or domains, which are the spheres of the contemplative knowledge.

What are these five? He says: adhilokam — the contemplation in respect of the worlds; likewise adhijyautiṣam (in respect of the luminaries), adhividyam (in respect of learning), adhiprajam (in respect of progeny), and adhyātmam (in respect of the body). Since these five upaniṣads have for their objects the great realities — the worlds and the rest — and have saṁhitā for their substrate, those who know the Veda call them ‘mahā-saṁhitās', the great unions.

Now, of these as just enumerated, the contemplation adhiloka is being declared; the word ‘atha' throughout marks the order in which the contemplations are to be presented. ‘Pṛthivī pūrva-rūpam' — the earth is the pūrva-rūpa, the prior form, that is, the first letter (pūrva varṇa); meaning, in the prior letter of the saṁhitā the contemplation of the earth (pṛthivī-dṛṣṭi) is to be done. So too ‘dyaur uttara-rūpam' — the heaven is the latter form, that is, the latter letter. ‘Ākāśaḥ sandhiḥ' — the antarikṣa-loka, the mid-region, is the sandhi, the junction, the middle in which the prior and the latter forms are joined together (sandhīyate).
T_C01_S03_V02: ‘Vāyu is the sandhāna (the conjoiner). Thus the adhiloka. Now adhijyautiṣam: Agni is the prior form; Āditya, the latter form; the waters are the sandhi; the lightning (vaidyutaḥ) is the conjoiner. Thus the adhijyautiṣam. Now adhividyam: the ācārya is the prior form…'
T_C01_S03_V03: ‘…the disciple (antevāsin) the latter form; the vidyā is the sandhi; the act of expounding (pravacanam) is the conjoiner. Thus the adhividyam. Now adhipraja: the mother is the prior form; the father is the latter form; the offspring (prajā) is the sandhi; the begetting (prajananam) is the conjoiner. Thus the adhiprajam.'
T_C01_S03_V04: ‘Now adhyātmam: the lower jaw is the prior form; the upper jaw the latter form; speech is the sandhi; the tongue is the conjoiner. Thus the adhyātmam. These are the mahā-saṁhitās. Whoever knows these mahā-saṁhitās thus expounded becomes united with progeny, with cattle, with brahma-varcas, with food and the eatable, and with the heavenly world.'
T_C01_S03_V04::block-0:
‘Vāyuḥ sandhānam' — vāyu is the sandhāna, the conjoiner; ‘sandhāna' is etymologised as ‘that by which (anena) it is conjoined' (sandhīyate). Thus has been declared the adhiloka contemplation. ‘Atha adhijyautiṣam', and the rest, follow on a parallel pattern (samāna), and need no fresh explanation.

‘Iti imāḥ' — ‘these (mahā-saṁhitās) thus declared' — the term ‘imāḥ' indicates that what has just been stated is now being held up for view (upapradarśyante).

Whoever, ‘evam' — exactly in this manner, ‘etāḥ mahā-saṁhitāḥ vyākhyātāḥ' — these mahā-saṁhitās as expounded — ‘veda' — knows; ‘knows' here is to be understood as ‘meditates upon' (upāsate). For ‘veda' may certainly mean ‘upāsana', because the context is one of contemplative knowledge (vijñāna-adhikāra), and because the very passage says, ‘iti prācīnayogyopāssva' — ‘O Prācīnayogya, meditate thus'.

Upāsana, moreover, is the unbroken stream of similar cognitions (tulya-pratyaya-santati), as enjoined by the śāstra, unmingled with cognitions of other things (atat-pratyayaiḥ asaṅkīrṇa), and directed upon the object prescribed by the śāstra. The meaning of upāsana is well known in worldly usage too: ‘He waits upon (upāste) the guru', ‘he waits upon the king' — for one who continually attends upon the guru and the like is said to ‘upāste'. And he obtains the fruit of his upāsana.

Hence here also, ‘he who knows thus' is sandhīyate — joined together, in turn, with progeny, cattle, brahma-varcas, food, and finally with the svarga-loka. The meaning is: he obtains the fruits beginning with progeny and ending with svarga.
T_C01_S04_V01: ‘He who is the bull of the metres, of universal form, who came forth from out of the immortal Vedic metres — may that Indra strengthen me with intelligence (medhā). May I, O God, be a bearer of the immortal! May my body be active (vicarṣaṇam); may my tongue be the most honeyed; may I hear abundantly through my ears! Thou art the sheath (kośa) of Brahman, covered over by intelligence; protect well what I have learnt. (She, the goddess of fortune,) bringing and spreading forth…'
T_C01_S04_V02: Achieving for myself, swiftly: clothes for me and cattle, food and drink always — bring me thereafter prosperity, woolly with cattle, svāhā. Let brahmacārins approach me, svāhā. Let brahmacārins come variously, svāhā. Let brahmacārins come abundantly, svāhā. Let brahmacārins come self-controlled, svāhā. Let brahmacārins come tranquil, svāhā.
T_C01_S04_V03: May I be glorious among men, svāhā. May I be more excellent than the wealthier, svāhā. May I, O Bhaga, enter into Thee, svāhā. May Thou, O Bhaga, enter into me, svāhā. In Thee of a thousand branches, O Bhaga, may I cleanse myself, svāhā. As waters flow downward, as months merge into the year, so, O Dhātṛ, let brahmacārins come to me from every side, svāhā. Thou art a refuge — be a light unto me; come to me, take me to Thyself.
T_C01_S04_V03::block-0:
‘Yaśchandasām’ — here are taught the japa and homa which are the means of attaining the desire of one who longs for medhā (intelligence) and for śrī (prosperity). The indications are evident in the texts ‘Sa māmindro medhayā spṛṇotu’ and ‘tato me śriyamāvaha’.

‘Yaḥ chandasām’ — among the chandas, that is, among the Vedas — ‘ṛṣabha iva’, like a bull, the foremost, by reason of pre-eminence. Here ‘chandas’ stands for the Vedas. ‘Viśvarūpaḥ’ — of all forms, since the Praṇava pervades all speech, as another śruti declares: ‘As all the leaves are pierced by a needle through the central rib, so all speech is pierced through by Oṁ; Oṁ alone is all this’ (Chā. Up. 2.23.3). For this very reason Oṁkāra is the bull. Since here Oṁkāra is the object of upāsana, it is fitting that words like ‘ṛṣabha’ should be terms of praise of Oṁkāra.

‘Chandobhyaḥ adhi’ — from the Vedas; for the Vedas are amṛta (immortal). From that immortal source, when Prajāpati, desiring to extract the very quintessence of the worlds, deities, Vedas, and the vyāhṛtis, performed tapas, Oṁkāra shone forth as that essence-most. This is the meaning. For of Oṁkāra, which is eternal, no actual origination is possible; ‘sambabhūva’ is to be construed as ‘shone forth’.

That very Oṁkāra, being ‘Indra’ — the supreme Lord, lord of all desires — ‘mā medhayā spṛṇotu’: may He gladden me with prajñā (insight), or strengthen me; for it is the strength of intelligence that is here prayed for. ‘Amṛtasya dhāraṇaḥ’ — may I be the sustainer of the immortal, that is, of the knowledge of Brahman, which is the cause of immortality, since I am qualified for it. ‘He deva’ — O resplendent one.

‘Śarīraṁ me vicarṣaṇam’ — may my body be capable, fit (for receiving the knowledge); the construction shifts from third person to first person. ‘Jihvā me madhumattamā’ — may my tongue be sweetest, supremely sweet of speech. ‘Karṇābhyāṁ bhūri viśruvam’ — may I hear much through the ears, may I be a great hearer. The whole import is: let this aggregate of body and organs be fit for the knowledge of the Self. And medhā too is prayed for solely with that aim.

‘Brahmaṇaḥ kośo'si’ — Thou art the kośa, the sheath, of the supreme Self, like the sheath of a sword, since Thou art the locus of the realisation of Brahman; Thou art the symbol (pratīka) of Brahman, in Thee Brahman is realised. ‘Medhayā pihitaḥ’ — covered over by ordinary, worldly intelligence; the inner truth of Thee remains unknown to those of common understanding. ‘Śrutaṁ me gopāya’ — protect for me what has been heard, namely the knowledge of the Self acquired through śravaṇa; that is, do that which prevents its being forgotten and ensures its attainment. These mantras are for japa, for one who desires medhā.

Now are taught the mantras meant for homa, for one who desires śrī. ‘Āvahantī’ — bringing; ‘vitanvānā’ — spreading out, since the root ‘tan’ has that as its action; ‘kurvāṇā’ — accomplishing; ‘acīram’ — quickly, swiftly (the long vowel being a Vedic peculiarity), or ‘ciram’ — for long. Accomplishing for me — ‘vāsāṁsi’, garments; ‘gāvaśca’, cattle; ‘annapāne ca sarvadā’, food and drink always. That śrī (prosperity) which accomplishes such things — ‘ṭataḥ āvaha’ — bring her after, that is, after the attainment of medhā; for to one without intelligence, śrī is only a source of misfortune.

Of what kind? ‘Lomaśām’ — possessed of woolly creatures, goats, sheep and the like; and ‘paśubhiḥ saha’ — together with cattle. ‘Bring her on’ — by virtue of the context, this is connected with Oṁkāra itself. ‘Svāhā’ — the utterance ‘svāhā’ marks the close of mantras meant for homa.

‘Āmāyantu’ — let them come to me; ‘mām’ is connected by separation with ‘āyantu’, namely, ‘brahmacāriṇaḥ’ — the brahmacārins. ‘Vimāyantu, pramāyantu, damāyantu, śamāyantu’ — let them come variously, abundantly, with self-control, and with tranquillity, and so on.

‘Yaśo jane'sāni’ — may I be famous among the renowned. ‘Śreyān’ — more praiseworthy; ‘vasyasaḥ’ — than the wealthier, than men of riches and rank — may I be one possessed of distinction beyond such people: that is the meaning. Further, ‘taṁ tvā’ — Thee, the kośa of Brahman; ‘he bhaga bhagavan’ — O Bhaga, worthy of worship; ‘praviśāni’ — may I enter; and having entered…
T_C01_S05_V01: ‘Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, Suvaḥ’ — these indeed are the three vyāhṛtis. Of them, the descendant of Mahācamasa knew yet a fourth — namely ‘Mahaḥ’. That is Brahman, that is the Self; the other deities are its limbs. ‘Bhūḥ’ verily is this world; ‘Bhuvaḥ’ is the mid-region; ‘Suvaḥ’ is yonder world.
T_C01_S05_V01::block-0: The upāsana relating to the saṁhitā has been taught. Following that, the mantras pertaining to one who desires medhā and śrī have been enumerated, and these too, by way of tradition, ultimately serve only the purpose of vidyā. Now, immediately, is introduced the inner upāsana of Brahman, which has the form of the vyāhṛtis, the fruit of which is svārājya (sovereignty).
T_C01_S05_V02: ‘Mahaḥ’ is the Sun (Āditya); for by the Sun indeed all worlds are exalted. ‘Bhūḥ’ verily is fire (Agni); ‘Bhuvaḥ’ is air (Vāyu); ‘Suvaḥ’ is the Sun; ‘Mahaḥ’ is the Moon (Candramas); for by the Moon indeed all luminaries are exalted. ‘Bhūḥ’ verily is the Ṛks; ‘Bhuvaḥ’ is the Sāmans; ‘Suvaḥ’ is the Yajuses.
T_C01_S05_V03: ‘Mahaḥ’ is Brahman; for by Brahman indeed all the Vedas are exalted. ‘Bhūḥ’ verily is prāṇa; ‘Bhuvaḥ’ is apāna; ‘Suvaḥ’ is vyāna; ‘Mahaḥ’ is food; for by food indeed all the prāṇas are exalted. These four, then, are each fourfold — four sets of four vyāhṛtis. He who knows them knows Brahman; to him all the gods bring tribute.
T_C01_S05_V03::block-0:
‘Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, Suvaḥ — iti’: the word ‘iti’ here is for the purpose of pointing out what was already mentioned. ‘Etāstisraḥ’ — these three — is the term that gathers up what was thus pointed out, the meaning being completed by ‘smaryante vai’ (‘they are indeed remembered’): these three well-known vyāhṛtis are recollected. Of them, this fourth vyāhṛti is ‘Mahaḥ’. That fourth vyāhṛti — ‘the descendant of Mahācamasa, the Māhācamasya, knew’; ‘u ha sma’ together has the force of narrating something past; that is, he had known, he had seen.

The mention of Māhācamasya is for the sake of recollecting the ṛṣi. Recollection of the ṛṣi too is understood to be an aṅga of upāsana, since it is enjoined here. That vyāhṛti ‘Mahaḥ’ which the Māhācamasya saw, is Brahman. For Brahman is mahat (great), and ‘Mahaḥ’ is the vyāhṛti.

What is it (more precisely)? ‘Sa ātmā’ — it is the Self; from the root ‘āp’, meaning ‘to pervade’. The other vyāhṛtis — namely the worlds, deities, Vedas and prāṇas — are pervaded by this vyāhṛti-self ‘Mahaḥ’ in the forms of Sun, Moon, Brahman and food. Therefore the other deities (and worlds and so on) are aṅgas, limbs. The mention of ‘deities’ is by way of upalakṣaṇa (suggestive indication) of worlds and the rest as well. Since the gods, worlds and the rest are limbs of this vyāhṛti-self ‘Mahaḥ’, hence it is said that worlds are exalted by Sun and so on. For limbs are exalted by the body. ‘Mahīyante’ — they grow, increase.

Thus we have: this world, fire, the Ṛgveda, prāṇa — this is the first vyāhṛti, ‘Bhūḥ’. The mid-region, air, the Sāmans, apāna — this is the second, ‘Bhuvaḥ’. Yonder world, the Sun, the Yajuses, vyāna — this is the third, ‘Suvaḥ’. The Sun, the Moon, Brahman, food — this is the fourth, ‘Mahaḥ’. Thus each becomes fourfold.

‘Mahaḥ iti brahma’ — Brahman here means Oṁkāra, since in the context of words (śabdādhikāra) nothing else is possible.

What else has been said is plain. ‘Tā vā etāścatasraścaturdhā’ — these very four, ‘Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, Suvaḥ, Mahaḥ’, are each in four ways; the word ‘dhā’ denotes mode. The meaning is, each of these four becomes fourfold. The repeated teaching of these vyāhṛtis, already enumerated, is for the sake of laying down the rule of upāsana of them in just that way. ‘Tāḥ … yo veda, sa veda’ — he who knows them as taught, knows.

Knows what? Brahman.

[Pūrvapakṣa:] But when Brahman has already been declared as ‘tad brahma, sa ātmā’, it should not be spoken of as if unknown — ‘he knows Brahman’. [Siddhānta:] No; the fault does not arise, for the intention is to set forth the special features (viśeṣa) of that very Brahman. Truly, by the fourth vyāhṛti it has been known that the Self is Brahman; but its special characteristics — being attainable within the heart, being mind-made (manomaya), and so forth, the entire group of attributes culminating in ‘śānti-samṛddham’ — have not yet been known. Wishing to teach these specific attributes, the śāstra speaks of Brahman as if not yet known and says ‘he knows Brahman’. Hence there is no defect.

The purport is: he who knows Brahman as qualified by the group of attributes about to be stated — he indeed knows Brahman. Hence this anuvāka is to be construed as one sentence with the following anuvāka, for both anuvākas have a single upāsana as their subject. The liṅga (indicatory mark) also confirms this: the statement ‘Bhūr ity agnau pratitiṣṭhati’ and the rest is the liṅga of the unity of upāsana. Moreover, no separate vidhāyaka (injunctive word) exists; for nowhere is there a word saying ‘know thus’ or ‘meditate thus’ as a fresh injunction. As for the words ‘tā yo veda’ in the vyāhṛti-anuvāka, since they refer to what is yet to be stated, they do not effect a separation of upāsanas. That they refer to what follows has just been shown by the argument that the special features are intended to be taught.

‘Sarve devāḥ asmai’ — to him who knows thus, all the gods, become his limbs, bring (āvahanti)…
T_C01_S06_V01: He who is this ākāśa within the heart — therein is this Person (Puruṣa), made of mind, immortal, golden. Between the two palates, that which hangs down like a nipple, that is the womb of Indra. Where the hair-end parts asunder, splitting open the cranium — by ‘Bhūḥ’ he stands firm in fire, by ‘Bhuvaḥ’ in air…
T_C01_S06_V01::block-0: It has been said that the worlds, deities and the rest, in the form of ‘Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, Suvaḥ’, are the limbs of this vyāhṛti-self Brahman, namely Hiraṇyagarbha denoted by ‘Mahaḥ’; and that the other deities are its limbs. Of that Brahman whose limbs they are, this very Brahman, for the sake of direct realisation and for the sake of upāsana, the ākāśa within the heart is now declared as its station — even as the śālagrāma stone is the station of Viṣṇu. For there alone, when meditated upon, that Brahman, qualified by manomayatva and the rest, is realised directly, like an āmalaka fruit on the palm. The path also for attaining the conviction of being the Self of all has to be told; hence this anuvāka is begun.
T_C01_S06_V02: By ‘Suvaḥ’ in the Sun, by ‘Mahaḥ’ in Brahman. He attains svārājya. He attains the Lord of the mind. Lord of speech, Lord of the eye, Lord of the ear, Lord of vijñāna he becomes. And further, this he becomes — ākāśa-bodied, true-natured Brahman, whose joy is in the prāṇas, whose mind is bliss, abounding in peace, immortal. Thus mayest thou meditate, O Prācīnayogya.
T_C01_S06_V02::block-0:
‘Saḥ’ — read with vyutkrama, this is connected with ‘ayaṁ puruṣaḥ’ that follows. ‘Ya eṣaḥ antarhṛdaye’ — within the heart. ‘Hṛdaya’ is the well-known lump of flesh shaped like a lotus, the seat of the prāṇas, riddled with many channels, with stalk upward and mouth downward, perceived in an animal when it is being cut open. Within it is this well-known ākāśa, like the ākāśa within a water-pot. ‘Tasmin’ — there is this ‘Puruṣa’, so called because of ‘puri śayanāt’ (lying in the city of the body), or because the worlds beginning with bhūḥ are filled (pūrṇāḥ) by Him.

‘Manomaya’ — composed of mind. The root ‘man’ takes ‘manas’ in the sense of cognition, since the root means ‘to know’; thus, that of which He is mostly made, since He is realised through it. Or ‘manas’ means the inner instrument by which one cognises; ‘manomaya’ then is one who identifies with that, or one who is indicated by that. ‘Amṛtaḥ’ — of immortal nature. ‘Hiraṇmayaḥ’ — full of light.

For the realisation of Him, of such characteristics, by the knower in whose heart-ākāśa He has been directly seen and who has become identified with Him in the form of the Lord, the path is now stated. From the heart upwards proceeds the channel called Suṣumnā, well known in the yoga-śāstras. It runs ‘antareṇa tālukī’ — between the two palates. That fleshy piece which hangs down like a nipple between the two palates — between that. ‘Yatra ca asau keśāntaḥ’ — where the root of the hairs (mūrdhan, the crown) parts asunder; reaching that region and forcing apart the cranium (śīrṣakapāla), splitting it open, having gone forth — that path ‘sā indrayoniḥ’ — that is the womb of Indra, that is, of Brahman; the womb is the path, the doorway for the realisation of His own nature.

The wise man who beholds the manomaya Self, having departed through the crown — by the vyāhṛti ‘Bhūḥ’, in the form of Agni who is the presiding deity of this world and the limb of the great Brahman, ‘pratitiṣṭhati’ — he stands firm in Agni; that is, he pervades this world in the form of Agni. Likewise by ‘Bhuvaḥ’ in Vāyu, the second vyāhṛti-self; ‘pratitiṣṭhati’ continues in connection. By ‘Suvaḥ’, the third, in Āditya; by ‘Mahaḥ’, the fourth and the aṅgin (possessor of the limbs), in Brahman, he stands firm. Standing thus as the very Self of them all, ‘āpnoti svārājyam’ — he attains svārājya, sovereignty in the form of Brahman; he himself becomes the king, the lord of the limb-deities, even as Brahman is. And to him, as to the aṅgin (the whole), all the gods bring tribute as limbs, just as they do to Brahman.

‘Āpnoti manasaspatim’ — He attains the lord of the mind, since Brahman is the lord of all minds, being the Self of all; for through all minds He cognises. The knower thus attains Him.

Further, he becomes ‘vākpati’, the lord of all speech; ‘cakṣuṣpati’, the lord of eyes; ‘śrotrapati’, the lord of ears; ‘vijñānapati’, the lord of vijñānas. Being of the nature of the Self of all, he becomes endowed with the organs of all beings: that is the meaning.

And more than this, he becomes this. What is that? It is now stated. ‘Ākāśa-śarīram’ — He whose body is ākāśa, or whose subtle body is like ākāśa. What? — the topical Brahman. ‘Satyātma’ — He whose self, that is, His real nature, is satya — the unfailing, both gross and subtle, mūrta and amūrta. ‘Prāṇārāmam’ — He whose play, whose sport, is in the prāṇas; or in whom the prāṇas have their resort. ‘Mana ānandam’ — He whose mind is verily of the form of ānanda, mind that produces only joy. ‘Śānti-samṛddham’ — abounding in śānti (peace, repose); peace itself is samṛddhi; or by śānti…
T_C01_S07_V01: Earth, mid-region, sky, the directions, the intermediate directions; fire, air, sun, moon, the constellations; waters, herbs, trees, ākāśa, the Self (the Virāṭ) — this is the adhibhūta (concerning beings). Now the adhyātma (concerning the self): prāṇa, vyāna, apāna, udāna, samāna; eye, ear, mind, speech, skin; skin, flesh, sinews, bones, marrow. Having so apportioned, the ṛṣi declared: ‘All this verily is fivefold (pāṅkta); by the fivefold (within) one fulfils the fivefold (without).’
T_C01_S07_V01::block-0: Of that vyāhṛti-self Brahman declared as the object of upāsana, now is set forth the upāsana in its very form as the pāṅkta beginning with earth and the rest.
T_C01_S07_V01::block-1:
By association with the number five (pañca-saṅkhyā-yogāt), the metre paṅkti is constituted; thence everything is pāṅkta. The yajña too is pāṅkta, as the śruti declares: ‘Paṅkti has five feet; the yajña is pāṅkta.’ Hence whatever is mentally constituted as pāṅkta — from the worlds down to the Self — that very thing is mentally constituted as the yajña. By the yajña thus constituted, one attains Prajāpati of the form pāṅkta.

How ‘all this is verily pāṅkta’ — to that he replies: Earth, mid-region, sky, directions, intermediate directions — this is the loka-pāṅkta. Fire, air, sun, moon, constellations — this is the devatā-pāṅkta. Waters, herbs, trees, ākāśa, Self — this is the bhūta-pāṅkta. ‘Ātmā’ here means Virāṭ, since the topic is bhūtas.

‘Ity adhibhūtam’ — this expression is upalakṣaṇa (suggestive) of the two pāṅktas concerning lokas and devatās as well, since the loka-pāṅkta and devatā-pāṅkta have indeed been mentioned (along with the bhūta-pāṅkta).

‘Atha’ — now, immediately following — three pāṅktas adhyātma are stated. Prāṇa and the rest — this is the vāyu-pāṅkta (the fivefold pertaining to the airs). Eye and the rest — this is the indriya-pāṅkta. Skin and the rest — this is the dhātu-pāṅkta. Just this much is all that is adhyātma and bāhya, and it is verily all pāṅkta — having thus apportioned (adhividhāya, parikalpya), the ṛṣi — i.e., the Veda, or some ṛṣi endowed with this insight — declared, spoke. What did he say? — ‘All this is verily pāṅkta; by the pāṅkta within (the adhyātmika), in virtue of common number, one fulfils, strengthens, completes the pāṅkta without (the bāhya), the meaning being: one apprehends them as one self.’ Thus, he who knows that ‘all this is pāṅkta’ becomes verily of the form of Prajāpati: that is the meaning.
T_C01_S08_V01: Om — this is Brahman. Om — this whole world is. Om — by this very syllable does one give consent: when summoned with ‘Cause to hear!’ they cause to hear with Om. With Om the udgātṛs sing the Sāmans. With ‘Om Śom’ the śastra-reciters chant the śastras. With Om the adhvaryu utters his pratigara-response. With Om the brahmā-priest grants his sanction. With Om one consents to the agnihotra. With Om the brāhmaṇa, about to recite, says — ‘May I attain Brahman!’ — and he does indeed attain Brahman.
T_C01_S08_V01::block-0: Earlier, the upāsanā of Brahman as the Self-of-the-vyāhṛtis was taught; thereafter, the same Brahman was made the object of upāsanā in its fivefold (pāṅkta) form. Now, with all upāsanās in view as their common limb, the upāsanā of the syllable Om is about to be enjoined.
T_C01_S08_V01::block-1: When meditated upon under the dṛṣṭi of the Higher and the lower Brahman, the syllable Om — though merely a sound — becomes the means of attaining the Higher and the lower Brahman alike; for it is the ālambana of both the supreme and the conditioned Brahman, just as the image is for Viṣṇu, as the śruti declares: ‘By this very support one attains the one or the other’ (Praśna 5.2). ‘Om iti’ — the word ‘iti’ serves to delimit the form: ‘this very sound-form Om is Brahman’ — thus one should hold it in the mind, that is, meditate upon it. For ‘Om — this whole world is’: the entirety of what is sound-natured is pervaded by Om, as another śruti puts it — ‘as by a peg’ (Chānd. 2.23.3). And since ‘the named is dependent on the naming-instrument’, ‘all this is Om’ is rightly said. The remainder of the passage is praise of Om, since Om is the upāsya. ‘Om iti anukṛtiḥ’ — Om is imitation: when one says ‘I shall do’ or ‘I shall go’, another consents by repeating Om; hence Om is anukṛti. The particles ‘ha sma vai’ indicate something well-known — for the imitative function of Om is famous. Further, on the prompt ‘O śrāvaya!’ they cause to hear, sounding back the response. Likewise, the sāma-singers sing the sāmans with Om. The śastra-reciters too chant śastras with ‘Om Śom’. So too the adhvaryu utters his pratigara with Om. With Om the brahmā-priest gives sanction — that is, grants assent. With Om he sanctions the agnihotra: when the offerer says ‘I offer’, the brahmā gives consent precisely with Om. The brāhmaṇa, when about to recite — that is, intending to begin study — utters Om: he takes up the act of recitation by Om alone; ‘May I attain Brahman, that is, the Veda; may I grasp it’ — and indeed he attains Brahman. Or else: ‘May I attain Brahman, the Supreme Self’ — about to deliver the Self, intending to convey it, he says only Om; and by that very Om he does attain Brahman. Since acts undertaken with Om at their head become fruit-bearing, therefore one should meditate on Om as Brahman — such is the import of the passage.
T_C01_S09_V01: Ṛta — and self-study and teaching. Truth — and self-study and teaching. Tapas — and self-study and teaching. Restraint of the outer senses — and self-study and teaching. Inner calm — and self-study and teaching. The sacred fires — and self-study and teaching. The agnihotra — and self-study and teaching. Hospitality to guests — and self-study and teaching. Conduct fitting to fellow men — and self-study and teaching. Offspring — and self-study and teaching. Procreation — and self-study and teaching. Continuation through grandchildren — and self-study and teaching. Satyavacas Rāthītara held: truth alone. Taponitya Pauruśiṣṭi held: tapas alone. Nāka Maudgalya held: just self-study and teaching — that indeed is tapas, that indeed is tapas.
T_C01_S09_V01::block-0: Since it has been said that ‘by knowledge alone one attains svārājya’, the seeming uselessness of the śrauta and smārta karmas threatens to follow. To prevent that, and to show that karmas serve as means to the puruṣārtha, this passage is here introduced —
T_C01_S09_V01::block-1: ‘Ṛta’ has already been explained. Svādhyāya is one's own Vedic study; pravacana is teaching others, or the brahmayajña. These — ṛta and the rest — must be performed; this is the supplied predicate. Satya is truth-telling, or speech aligned with the established sense. Tapas is the kṛcchra and the rest. Dama is the quieting of the outer instruments; śama, of the inner instrument. The sacred fires must be installed; the agnihotra offered; guests honoured. ‘Mānuṣa’ is everyday social conduct, to be carried out as the occasion demands. Offspring must be begotten; prajana is the act of begetting — that is, approaching one's wife in the season; prajāti is the birth of grandsons — meaning that one's son too must be settled in marriage. Even for one engaged in all these karmas, svādhyāya and pravacana must be performed with effort; that is why svādhyāya-pravacana is mentioned alongside each. For the meaning of the texts depends on svādhyāya, and the highest good depends on the meaning's knowledge; pravacana, in turn, prevents forgetting and increases dharma. Therefore one must take pains over both. ‘Satyam iti’ — Satyavacas Rāthītara — he whose speech is truth itself, or one named so, of the gotra of Rathītara — holds that truth alone is to be performed. ‘Tapa iti’ — Taponitya Pauruśiṣṭi — devoted constantly to tapas, or so named, son of Puruśiṣṭa — holds that tapas alone is to be done. ‘Just self-study and teaching’ — Nāka Maudgalya, son of Mudgala, holds that these alone are to be performed: ‘that indeed is tapas, that indeed is tapas’; since svādhyāya and pravacana are themselves tapas, they alone are to be enacted. The repeated mention of satya, tapas, and svādhyāya-pravacana — though already named — is for emphasis.
T_C01_S10_V01: I am the impeller of the tree (of saṃsāra). My fame is lofty as a mountain's ridge. Pure at my apex — like the Sun bearing his nourishing radiance — I am the splendid immortal Self. I am wealth bright with lustre. I am wise, deathless, undecaying. — Such was the Vedic recitation of Triśaṅku.
T_C01_S10_V01::block-0: ‘I am the impeller of the tree’ — this is a mantra-text intended for svādhyāya. From the topic, that svādhyāya is for the arising of vidyā: this whole section is for the sake of vidyā, no other purpose can be discerned. By svādhyāya the sattva is purified, and in such a one the rise of vidyā becomes intelligible. ‘I am the impeller of the tree’ — of the cuttable saṃsāra-tree, I, as antaryāmin-Self, am the impeller. ‘My kīrti — fame — is uplifted like a mountain-ridge.’ ‘Ūrdhvapavitra’ — he whose purifier set on high is the supreme Brahman, knowable through the light of jñāna, the cause of all — that all-Self I am: I am Ūrdhvapavitra. ‘Vājinīva’ — like the bearer of vāja, food: like the Sun who bears nourishment. As in the Sun the immortal Self-truth is well-known, pure, attested by hundreds of śrutis and smṛtis, so I am ‘su-amṛtam’ — the splendid, the pure Ātma-truth. ‘Draviṇaṃ savarcasam’ — wealth bright with lustre — that very Ātma-truth I am: ‘am’ continues. Or else, the Brahman-knowledge — being a revealer of the Ātma-truth — is ‘savarcas’; it is wealth-like, since it is the cause of mokṣa-bliss. On this reading one must supply ‘has been won by me’. ‘Sumedhāḥ’ — he of whom the medhā, marked by omniscience, is excellent — he is sumedhas; through the skill of creating, sustaining, and dissolving saṃsāra, I have sumedhastva. Hence I am ‘amṛta’, undying; ‘akṣita’, undecayed, unspent, imperishable, unwounded — or sprinkled with amṛta, as the brāhmaṇa says: ‘amṛtokṣito 'ham’ and so on. ‘Iti’ — thus is the vedānuvacana of the seer Triśaṅku, who, being a Brahman-knower, has himself become Brahman. Veda is vedana, the realisation of the oneness of the Ātman; speaking that follows upon its attainment is vedānuvacana. As with Vāmadeva, this mantra, beheld by Triśaṅku in seer-vision, declares his own state of having done all that is to be done — it makes plain Ātma-vidyā. The chanting of it is also understood to aid the rise of vidyā: this is gathered from its placement after the dharma-list of ‘Ṛtaṃ ca’ and the heading ‘vedānuvacana’. So, in one engaged in nitya śrauta-smārta karmas, free from desire, eager to know the supreme Brahman, ārṣa-darśanas concerning the Self and the like spontaneously arise.
T_C01_S11_V01: Having taught the Veda, the ācārya instructs the resident pupil: Speak truth. Practise dharma. Do not be remiss in self-study. Having brought to the ācārya the wealth dear to him, do not cut the thread of progeny. From truth one must not swerve. From dharma one must not swerve. From the auspicious one must not swerve. From prosperity one must not swerve. From self-study and teaching one must not swerve.
T_C01_S11_V02: From the duties to gods and forefathers one must not swerve. Be one to whom the mother is a god. Be one to whom the father is a god. Be one to whom the ācārya is a god. Be one to whom the guest is a god. Those acts that are blameless — those alone are to be cultivated, no others. Those of our own deeds that are well done — those alone you must hold up as your model.
T_C01_S11_V03: Not the others. Whatever brāhmaṇas are nobler than ourselves — for them you must furnish a seat for repose. Give with śraddhā. Do not give without śraddhā. Give in proportion to your means. Give with modesty. Give with awe. Give with fellowship. And then, if there should arise in you doubt about an action or doubt about a course of conduct —
T_C01_S11_V04: — those brāhmaṇas there who are reflective, well-judging, unattached, free from harshness, lovers of dharma — as they would conduct themselves in such a case, so should you conduct yourself there. So too in matters of accusation: as those reflective, well-judging, unattached, dharma-loving brāhmaṇas conduct themselves towards such persons, so should you conduct yourself towards them. This is the command. This is the teaching. This is the upaniṣad of the Veda. This is the discipline. Thus must one meditate. Thus indeed must this be meditated upon.
T_C01_S11_V04::block-0:
‘Vedam anūcya’ — here begins the teaching of duties; its purport is that, prior to the rise of Brahman-Self-knowledge, the śrauta and smārta karmas must be performed as a matter of rule, since this passage of instruction is meant for the saṃskāra of the person. For in the saṃskṛta — the one whose sattva has become pure — Self-knowledge arises with ease. Smṛti confirms: ‘By tapas one slays sin; by vidyā one attains the immortal’ (Manu 12.104). And further on the upaniṣad will say: ‘Seek to know Brahman by tapas’ (Tait. 3.2.1). Hence the karmas are to be performed for the rise of vidyā. From the very word ‘anuśāsti’ — ‘instructs’ — it follows that overstepping the instruction breeds fault. From the placement of the karma-list before, and before the start of the Brahman-vidyā proper, the karmas have been laid out. When Brahman-vidyā has dawned, on the other hand, the text will display niṣkiñcanatā — freedom from karmic involvement — through ‘he finds the fearless ground’ (Tait. 2.7.1), ‘he is afraid of nothing’ (Tait. 2.9.1), ‘why have I not done good?’ (Tait. 2.9.1), and the like. From all this we gather that karmas serve the rise of vidyā by way of destroying previously accumulated demerit. The mantra also says: ‘Crossing death by avidyā, by vidyā one attains the immortal’ (Īśā 11). The earlier mention of ṛta and the rest was to ward off their seeming pointlessness; here, since their bearing is on the rise of jñāna, it fixes them as duties.

‘Having taught the Veda, the ācārya instructs the antevāsin pupil’ — having had the text learnt, ‘anu’, that is, afterwards, he teaches its meaning, that is, makes the pupil grasp it. From this we gather that the student of the Veda must not return home from the gurukula without first inquiring into dharma; smṛti corroborates: ‘Knowing his rites, let him perform them.’ How does he instruct? — ‘Speak truth — speak what is to be spoken, as ascertained by pramāṇa. Practise dharma’ — dharma being the general name of all duties to be performed, since the particulars are mentioned separately. ‘From svādhyāya — recitation — do not stray.’ ‘Bringing wealth dear to the ācārya for the discharge of the vidyā-debt, and being permitted by him to take a fitting wife, do not cut the thread of progeny’ — the line of descendants must not be severed; even if a son is not born, one must strive by the putrakāmā and other rites for his birth — this is the import, since prajā, prajana, and prajāti are all listed (else only ‘prajana’ would have sufficed). ‘From truth one must not swerve’ — swerving from truth amounts to falsehood; the very word ‘pramāda’ shows that even out of forgetfulness one must not utter what is untrue, otherwise the injunction would have been a bare prohibition of false speech. ‘From dharma one must not swerve’ — since dharma here means the specific duties, non-performance is pramāda; dharma is to be enacted. So too — ‘from the kuśala’ (the auspicious, that which protects the Self) one must not swerve. ‘Bhūti’ is prosperity; from karmas conducive to prosperity and well-being one must not swerve. ‘From svādhyāya and pravacana one must not swerve’ — these two are obligatory by rule. So too with the rites for the gods and forefathers — they must be done. ‘Mātṛdevaḥ’ — he whose god is the mother — be such; so too pitṛdevaḥ, ācāryadevaḥ, atithidevaḥ.
T_C01_S11_V04::block-1:
Here it is examined, for the sake of distinguishing vidyā and karma — does the highest good come from karmas alone, or from karmas joined with vidyā, or from vidyā and karma in fusion, or from vidyā that needs karma, or from vidyā alone?

‘From karmas alone’ — for one who knows the entire Veda's meaning is qualified for karma; smṛti: ‘The whole Veda, with its secret, must be mastered by the twice-born.’ And ‘mastery’ includes knowledge of the upaniṣadic content, namely Self-knowledge. ‘The knower sacrifices’, ‘the knower causes others to sacrifice’ — everywhere it is shown that adhikāra in karma is precisely for the knower, and that one acts after knowing. Some hold that the entire Veda is for karma. If the highest good is not won from karmas, the Veda would be useless.

No. — Mokṣa is held to be eternal. The product of karma is in the world known to be non-eternal. If mokṣa came from karmas, it would be non-eternal — an unwelcome consequence.

Objection: One could refrain from kāmya and pratiṣiddha karmas; what has begun is exhausted by experience; performance of nityas precludes pratyavāya — so mokṣa results without dependence on jñāna. — That has already been answered: a residue of karma must remain, and through it another body comes about, so saṃsāra is not avoided; nor is the residue exhausted by nitya-anuṣṭhāna — there is no contradiction between nitya-karma and the residue.

As to the claim that ‘knowledge of the entire Veda's meaning makes one fit for karma’, that does not stand: upāsana stands apart from textual knowledge. By bare hearing of the text one becomes qualified for karma; one need not wait upon upāsana-jñāna. Upāsana is enjoined as something other than mere hearing, with mokṣa as its fruit; ‘He is to be heard’ — and then, distinct from this, ‘he is to be reflected upon, deeply meditated upon’ — these are separate efforts; manana and nididhyāsana are well known to differ from hearing and from informational knowing.

Then perhaps mokṣa comes from karmas with vidyā as their auxiliary. Karmas joined with vidyā might have the power to bring about a wholly new effect — just as poison, curd, and the rest, naturally productive of death or fever, when joined with mantra, sugar, etc., produce other effects; so karmas energised by vidyā might begin mokṣa. — No, the same fault remains: a thing that is begun is non-eternal. — But by an explicit text it can be both begun and eternal! — No: scripture is jñāpaka. A vacana makes known what is, not what is non-existent; not by a hundred texts can a thing be ‘begun and yet eternal’; nor would something that has been begun escape destruction. By this same argument the doctrine that vidyā and karma in fusion begin mokṣa is also rejected.
T_C01_S11_V04::block-2:
Suppose vidyā and karma jointly remove the obstacles to mokṣa. — No: karma's fruit is otherwise seen. Karma's fruits are observed to be utpatti, vikāra, saṃskāra, and āpti; and mokṣa is contrary to all four.

But the gati-śrutis make it āpya — ‘by the path of the Sun’, ‘by these two ascending’ (Kaṭha 2.3.16) — so mokṣa is to be reached. — No: Brahman is all-pervading and the goer is not other than it. Brahman is all-pervading because it is the cause of ākāśa and the rest, and the vijñāna-ātmans are not separate from Brahman; therefore mokṣa is not ‘to be reached’. The ‘to-be-reached’ is other than the goer and resident in another place. Where there is no separation, there is no ‘going’. The non-separation is established by hundreds of śruti-smṛti-vacanas: ‘having created it, into that very thing he entered’ (Tait. 2.6.1), ‘know me too as the kṣetrajña in all bodies’ (Gītā 13.2), and so on.

Objection: But then there would be conflict with the śrutis on going and lordship — ‘he becomes one’ (Chānd. 7.26.2), ‘if he desires the world of fathers’ (Chānd. 8.2.1), ‘with women, vehicles’ (Chānd. 8.12.3), etc. — No: those refer to the kārya-Brahman. In the kārya-Brahman women and the rest are possible, not in the kāraṇa, since ‘one only, without a second’ (Chānd. 6.2.1), ‘where one sees no other’ (Chānd. 7.24.1), ‘there by what would one see what?’ (Bṛh. 2.4.14; 4.5.15) and so on.

Moreover, by reason of conflict, vidyā and karma cannot be combined. Vidyā, whose object is the truth in which the special factors of agent and action have been resolved, is opposed to karma, which is to be effected through these very factors taken contrariwise. One and the same thing cannot, in truth, be seen as both possessing and devoid of agent etc.; one of the two must be illusory. And when one of the two has to be admitted as illusory, what is fitting is that the duality, the object of innate ignorance, is illusory — by hundreds of śrutis: ‘where there is duality, as it were’ (Bṛh. 2.4.14), ‘he goes from death to death’ (Kaṭha 2.1.10; Bṛh. 4.4.19), ‘where one sees another, that is the small’ (Chānd. 7.24.1), ‘he is other, I am other’ (Bṛh. 1.4.10), ‘he makes a chink within’, ‘then for him there is fear’ (Tait. 2.7.1), and so on. The reality of oneness is established by ‘in but one way is it to be seen’ (Bṛh. 4.4.20), ‘one only, without a second’ (Chānd. 6.2.1), ‘all this is Brahman alone’, ‘all this is the Self alone’ (Chānd. 7.25.2). Where the differences of recipient etc. — the kāraka-distinctions — are not seen, karma is not possible. Refutations of otherness-perception are heard by the thousand in the vidyā-context. Hence vidyā and karma are in conflict, and their combination is impossible.
T_C01_S11_V04::block-3:
As to the further claim that mokṣa comes from karma joined with vidyā, that is unsound — and the objection that ‘the texts that enjoin karma would conflict’ is also unfounded. If Self-oneness-knowledge were enjoined as overturning the very factors of agency etc., as the rope-knowledge overturns the snake-illusion, then the karma-vidhi-śrutis would be left without object — they would clash. But karmas have indeed been enjoined; and this conflict, you object, is unbearable, given the authority of the śrutis. — No, for the śrutis aim at instructing in the puruṣārtha. The śruti aims at vidyā: ‘the puruṣa must be liberated from saṃsāra; the avidyā that is the cause of saṃsāra must be removed by vidyā’ — proceeding in this aim, it lights up vidyā; hence no conflict.

Even so, the śāstra, which establishes the existence of agent and the like, is nullified! — No: scripture, taking up the existence of factors as already given, ordains karmas for the destruction of accumulated demerit, and, for those who seek mokṣa or who seek other ends, prescribes the means to those ends — it does not undertake to establish the very existence of the kārakas. For one whose karmic obstacle is dense, vidyā cannot dawn; with its destruction vidyā arises; with vidyā, avidyā ceases; with that, the absolute cessation of saṃsāra. Further, only one who sees the non-Self has desire turned upon the non-Self; desiring, he does karma; from that, for the sake of enjoying its fruit, comes saṃsāra characterised by the taking-on of bodies. Apart from that, for one who sees the oneness of the Self, there is no object, hence no kāma; and where there is non-difference within the Self, with kāma impossible, the abiding in one's own Self is mokṣa — so vidyā and karma are at variance from this side too. From this very conflict, vidyā does not, with regard to mokṣa, depend on karmas. But for the gaining of one's own Self, by way of removing the obstacle of previously accumulated demerit, the nitya-karmas come to be a means towards vidyā. That is precisely why we said that the karmas have been laid out in this section. Thus the karma-vidhi-śrutis are in no conflict. Therefore, the highest good is from vidyā alone — siddha.
T_C01_S11_V04::block-4:
Then it would follow that the other āśramas have no purpose: since the rise of vidyā is occasioned by karma, and the karmas are enjoined for the householder, only one āśrama would stand. The yāvajjīva-śrutis (‘all life long’) would then be most congenial. — No: for there are many karmas. Not only the agnihotra and the like; brahmacarya, tapas, satya-vacana, śama, dama, ahiṃsā, and so forth — well-known in the other āśramas — are unmixed and most apt for vidyā's arising; so too dhyāna, dhāraṇā, and the rest. The text will say: ‘Seek to know Brahman by tapas’ (Tait. 3.2.1). Vidyā can arise even before householdership through karmas done in past births; householdership is itself entered for the sake of karma; once vidyā can be had through means already at hand, entry into householder life becomes purposeless. Sons and so on are for the sake of the worlds; by the man who has turned away from the desire for the worlds attained through sons — ‘this world, the world of fathers, the world of gods’ — by him who sees the ever-perfect Self, who sees no purpose in karma, how can engagement be possible? Even one who has entered the householder stage, on the rise of vidyā and its ripening, becoming dispassionate and seeing no point in karmas, will turn away from them — as the śruti hints: ‘I am about to wander forth from this state, O dear’ (Bṛh. 4.5.2).

— ‘But the śruti shows greater effort towards karma; so this is unwarranted.’ — Towards the agnihotra and so on the śruti makes greater effort, and the labour in karma is great, since they require many means; tapas, brahmacarya, and the duties of the other āśramas are equally available within householdership and need fewer means; therefore the option for the āśramin is not on a par. — No: by the favour of acts done in another life. What you said about the greater effort in karma is no fault: the agnihotra-class karma and the brahmacarya-class observance done in past births also help towards the rise of vidyā in this life; some are seen dispassionate from the very birth, others are engaged in karmas, undispassionate, hostile to vidyā. Hence those rendered dispassionate by saṃskāras of past lives do enter another āśrama. Further, on account of the multitude of karma-fruits — sons, heaven, brahma-varcas — innumerable, and corresponding to the multitude of human desires, the śruti makes greater effort towards karma; the multitude of formula-prayers (‘may this be mine, may this be mine’) shows it. And because karmas are means: we have said that karmas are means with regard to vidyā; on the means greater effort is right, not on the end. — ‘But if karma occasions vidyā, then any further effort at upaniṣad-hearing etc. is purposeless.’ — No, for there is no rule. There is no rule that ‘vidyā arises only from the destruction of obstacles, never from īśvara-prasāda, tapas, dhyāna, or any other observance’; ahiṃsā, brahmacarya, and the rest do help vidyā, while śravaṇa, manana, nididhyāsana are direct causes. Therefore the other āśramas are established. And all are eligible for vidyā, [the Supreme] —
T_C01_S12_V01: May Mitra be peace to us, may Varuṇa be peace. May Aryaman be peace to us. May Indra and Bṛhaspati be peace to us. May Viṣṇu of wide strides be peace to us. Salutation to Brahman. Salutation to thee, Vāyu. Thou alone art the visible Brahman. Thee alone have I called the visible Brahman. I have spoken Ṛta. I have spoken Truth. May that protect me. May that protect the speaker. May it protect me. May it protect the speaker.
T_C01_S12_V01::block-0: He recites the śānti for the quelling of any obstacle to the vidyā already attained —
T_C01_S12_V01::block-1: ‘Śaṃ no mitraḥ’ — this and the rest. It has been explained earlier.
T_C02_S01_V00: Om. May He protect us both together; may He nourish us both together; may we both work together with vigour; may our study be illuminating; may we never hate each other. Om. Peace, peace, peace.
T_C02_S01_V00::block-0: Leading bhāṣya. The earlier śānti-pāṭha was recited for the pacification of obstacles to the attainment of the vidyā that has already been treated. Now, however, this śānti is recited for the pacification of obstacles to the attainment of the brahma-vidyā that is about to be expounded —
T_C02_S01_V00::block-1:
Bhāṣya on the mantra. ‘Saha nāv avatu' — May He, the Lord, protect us both, the pupil and the teacher, together (saha eva, jointly). ‘Saha nau bhunaktu' — May Brahman feed us both, that is, may He cause us to enjoy the fruit of vidyā together. ‘Saha vīryaṁ karavāvahai' — May we both together accomplish (nirvartayāvahai) the energy (sāmarthya) which arises by reason of the vidyā. ‘Tejasvi nāv adhītam astu' — May what we two have studied be ‘tejasvi', that is, may it become fit (yogya) for the apprehension of its meaning, well-mastered (svadhītam) by us, the two who are tejasvinau.

‘Mā vidviṣāvahai' — Through the pramāda (carelessness, lapse) of either pupil or teacher, an unjustified (anyāya) cause for hatred (vidveṣa) might arise on account of the very process of receiving the vidyā; for the pacification of that, this benediction is uttered: ‘Mā vidviṣāvahai' — May we two never come to mutually hate each other.

The threefold utterance ‘śāntiḥ śāntiḥ śāntiḥ' has the meaning already explained (the warding off of the ādhyātmika, ādhibhautika and ādhidaivika obstacles). And this śānti is for the pacification of the obstacles to the vidyā about to be set forth: it is precisely the unobstructed attainment of ātma-vidyā that is here desired, since it is the very root of the supreme good (paraṁ śreyas).
T_C02_S01_V01: The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme. As to that, this verse has been declared: ‘Brahman is satya, jñāna, ananta. He who knows It as set down in the cave (guhā), in the highest ākāśa, he obtains all desires together with Brahman, the Wise.' From this Self, verily, ākāśa came forth; from ākāśa, vāyu; from vāyu, agni; from agni, the waters; from the waters, the earth; from the earth, the herbs; from the herbs, food; from food, puruṣa. This puruṣa is verily formed of the essence of food (anna-rasa-maya). Of him this is verily the head; this is the right wing; this is the left wing; this is the trunk (ātman); this lower part is the tail, the support (pratiṣṭhā). Concerning that, there is also this verse:
T_C02_S01_V01::block-0: Leading bhāṣya. The upāsanās relating to the saṁhitā etc., not in conflict with karma, have been set forth. Next, with sopādhika ātma-darśana — accompanied by the upādhis — has been taught through the vyāhṛtis, with svārājya as its fruit. But by that much, the seed of saṁsāra in its entirety is not uprooted. Therefore, for the cessation of avidyā — the seed of all calamity — and for the realisation of the Self stripped of every upādhi, this section is now begun.
T_C02_S01_V01::block-1:
Bhāṣya. ‘Brahmavid āpnoti param', etc. The fruit of this brahma-vidyā is the cessation of avidyā, and thence the absolute cessation of saṁsāra. The text will say: ‘The knower fears nothing whatsoever' (Tai. Up. 2.9.1). If the cause of saṁsāra still remained, it would be impossible to ‘find fearlessness as one's foundation', and the words ‘he is not tormented by the question whether he has done or not done good and evil' would also be unintelligible. Hence, from this knowledge whose object is the all-Self Brahman, the absolute cessation of saṁsāra is established.

The śruti itself states the prayojana at the very beginning by ‘brahmavid āpnoti param', so as to make known the relation (sambandha) and purpose (prayojana). Once these are ascertained, one engages in the hearing, grasping, retention and repeated contemplation (śravaṇa-grahaṇa-dhāraṇābhyāsa) of the vidyā; for the fruit of vidyā follows śravaṇa etc., as in ‘He is to be heard, reflected upon, meditated upon' (Bṛ. Up. 2.4.5).

‘Brahmavit' — he who knows Brahman, of the lakṣaṇa about to be stated; ‘Brahman' is so called from being bṛhattama, the largest. He attains the param, the unsurpassed; that very Brahman is param. There is no question of the attainment of one thing by knowing another. The other śruti makes the attainment of Brahman by the knower of Brahman manifest: ‘He who knows that supreme Brahman becomes Brahman itself' (Mu. Up. 3.2.9).
T_C02_S02_V01: From food, verily, are creatures born — whatever creatures dwell upon the earth. Then by food alone do they live; and at the end, into food they enter again. For food is the eldest of beings; therefore it is called sarvauṣadham (the universal medicine). All food, verily, do they obtain who worship food as Brahman. For food is the eldest of beings; therefore it is called sarvauṣadham. From food beings are born; once born, they grow by food; it is eaten by beings, and itself eats them — therefore it is called ‘anna' (food). From this anna-rasa-maya self, different and inner, is another self, the prāṇamaya. By that, this is filled. He too has the form of a person. Following the human form of the former, this one too is human in form. Of him, prāṇa is the head; vyāna the right wing; apāna the left wing; ākāśa the trunk; the earth, pratiṣṭhā, the tail. Concerning that, there is also this verse:
T_C02_S02_V01::block-0:
Bhāṣya. ‘Annāt vai prajāḥ' — From food, transformed into rasa and the rest, prajāḥ, the entire mobile and immobile creation, are born. ‘Vai' is for recollection. ‘Yāḥ kāś ca pṛthivīṁ śritāḥ' — whatever creatures, without any exception, are sheltered upon the earth — they are all born from food alone. ‘Atho' — ‘moreover'; once born, they live (jīvanti) — sustain their prāṇas, that is, grow — by food alone. ‘Atho' again — at the end, when the activity called ‘living' is finished, they enter (apiyanti) into food itself: ‘api' here is in the sense of ‘prati' — they merge back into food.

Why? Because food is the eldest, the first-born of beings; for food is the cause of the annamaya and other beings. Hence all creatures are anna-prabhava (born of food), anna-jīvana (living by food), anna-pralaya (dissolved into food). And because so, food is called sarvauṣadham — for food is what assuages the burning of the body in all beings.
T_C02_S02_V01::block-1:
Bhāṣya. The fruit for the worshipper of anna-as-Brahman is now stated: ‘Sarvaṁ vai te annam āpnuvanti' — they obtain all the variety of food, who worship anna as Brahman in the manner taught: ‘I am born of food, my self is food, my dissolution is in food; therefore food is Brahman.' Why does the worship of food-as-self yield the obtaining of all food? Because anna is the eldest, born before all beings; hence ‘sarvauṣadham' — and the obtaining of all food by such an upāsaka is intelligible. The repetition ‘annād bhūtāni jāyante, jātāny annena vardhante' is for the upasaṁhāra (concluding restatement).

Now the etymology of anna is given: it is eaten (adyate, bhujyate) by beings, and it itself eats (atti) beings — being eaten by beings and being the eater of beings — therefore it is called anna. ‘Iti' marks the close of the first kośa.

The śāstra now wishes to show, by means of the vidyā, the inmost Brahman as the prati-yag-ātman, peeling away the five kośas — annamaya through ānandamaya — that have been fashioned by avidyā, just as one removes the husks of many koḍrava grains to reach the rice. So it begins: ‘Tasmād vā etasmād annarasamayāt'. From this annarasamaya body, different (anya) and inner (antara), is another self — the prāṇamaya — falsely imagined as a self, just like the body. Prāṇa is vāyu; tan-maya means tat-prāya, having that as its substance. By this prāṇamaya, the annarasamaya self is filled, as a leather bag is filled by air. This prāṇamaya self too is puruṣa-vidha — having the form of a person, with head and wings.

Is it so by itself? No. The puruṣa-form of the annarasamaya is well known. Following (anu) that puruṣa-form, this prāṇamaya is shaped as a person — like an image cast in a mould, not by itself. So in each succeeding kośa: each successor takes the form of its predecessor; and each predecessor is filled by its successor.

How is the puruṣa-form here? ‘Tasya prāṇa eva śiraḥ' — of the prāṇamaya self, which is a modification of vāyu, the prāṇa — the breathing-out activity issuing from mouth and nostrils — is imagined as the head, by śruti's own statement; everywhere these limb-imaginations rest on the express word of the text. Vyāna, the diffusing breath, is the right wing; apāna, the down-going, the left wing. ‘Ākāśa is ātmā' — that vṛtti named samāna which abides in the inner ākāśa is the trunk, since the topic concerns prāṇa-vṛttis: the central one, with the others around it as limbs, becomes ‘ātmā' — the middle, by śruti, ‘mid-most of these limbs is the ātmā'. ‘Pṛthivī pucchaṁ pratiṣṭhā' — Pṛthivī as deity is the support of the bodily prāṇa, sustaining it, as the other śruti says, ‘She, taking hold of the apāna of man, supports him' (Pra. Up. 3.8); else, by udāna's upward draw or by mere weight, the body would either rise or fall. ‘Tad apy eṣa śloko bhavati' — on this very subject of the prāṇamaya self, this verse occurs.
T_C02_S03_V01: After prāṇa the gods breathe — and so do men and beasts. For prāṇa is the life of beings; therefore it is called sarvāyuṣam (the life of all). They obtain a full life-span who worship prāṇa as Brahman; for prāṇa is the life of beings, therefore called sarvāyuṣam. The embodied self of the former (annamaya) is this very prāṇamaya. From this prāṇamaya self, different and inner, is another self — the manomaya. By it, this is filled. He too has the form of a person. Following the human form of the former, this is human in form. Of him, the head is yajus; the right wing ṛk; the left wing sāman; the trunk is ādeśa (the brāhmaṇa); the tail, the foundation, is the Atharvāṅgirasas. Concerning that, there is also this verse:
T_C02_S03_V01::block-0:
Bhāṣya. ‘Prāṇaṁ devā anu prāṇanti.' Agni and the other gods, having prāṇa — the vāyu-natured, possessor of breathing power — as their inner soul, breathe (perform the activity of prāṇana) following him. Since the topic is adhyātma, ‘devāḥ' here means the indriyas: the senses too perform their activity following the prāṇa, or, alternatively, ‘follow the chief prāṇa in their movements'. So too men and beasts; they too move because of the action called prāṇana. Hence creatures are not embodied merely by the limited annamaya self; they are also embodied by that which is internal to it — the prāṇamaya, the common one, pervading every body. So men and the rest are embodied successively by the still finer manomaya etc., culminating in ānandamaya — all begotten of avidyā out of ākāśa and the elements. And finally they are embodied by the natural cause of all — the eternal, unmodified, all-pervading Self of the lakṣaṇa ‘sat-jñāna-ananta', which transcends the five kośas. So that one is in truth the Self of all — that too is implicitly stated.

Why is it said ‘the gods breathe after prāṇa'? Because prāṇa is the āyus (life) of beings, as another śruti says: ‘So long as prāṇa dwells in this body, so long indeed is its life' (Kauṣ. Up. 3.2). Hence ‘sarvāyuṣam' — the life of all is sarvāyus, and that itself is sarvāyuṣam — for the moment prāṇa departs, death ensues; in worldly experience too the universal life-giving role of prāṇa is well known. Therefore, abandoning the external annamaya — which is uncommon (asādhāraṇa) — one should worship the inner, common prāṇamaya self as Brahman, with the conviction ‘I am prāṇa, the self of all beings, their life'. Such worshippers obtain the full life-span in this world, and do not perish by untimely death (apamṛtyu) before the natural span. ‘A hundred years' is the proper span, by ‘sarvam āyur eti' (Chā. Up. 2.11.2; 4.11.2). The repetition ‘prāṇo hi bhūtānām…' is for the establishing of the cause of fruit: he who worships Brahman with such-and-such qualities partakes of those qualities.

The śārīra ātmā of the former (annamaya) — dwelling in the annamaya body — is this very prāṇamaya. ‘Tasmād vā etasmāt' etc. has the meaning already given. ‘Anya, antara ātmā manomaya' — manas, the inner organ marked by saṅkalpa-vikalpa; what is composed of it (tan-maya) is manomaya, the self interior to prāṇamaya. ‘Of him, yajus alone is the head' — yajus is the type of mantra without fixed syllables and metrical pādas; the word yajus stands for that class. It is the head because of its primacy: in the yāgādi rituals it is the principal ‘sannipatya-upakāraka' — by the yajus, accompanied by ‘svāhā' etc., the oblation is given.
T_C02_S03_V01::block-1:
The imagination of head etc. is everywhere by śruti's express statement (vācanikī). The vṛtti of the manas — the activity (saṅkalpa-imagined, mental-rooted) which has as its objects the sthāna, prayatna, nāda, svara, varṇa, pada and vākya — is called ‘yajus' as marked off by the convention ‘yajus' through the door of the ear. Likewise ‘ṛk' and ‘sāman'. Mantras being thus mano-vṛttis, the vṛtti itself is repeated; hence mānasa-japa is intelligible. Otherwise, mantras being non-objects, they could not be repeated like a pot — and mānasa-japa would be impossible. The mantra-āvṛtti is enjoined many times in karmas; if one were to take the repetition as merely the recurrence of memory of syllables, the primary sense would be lost.

Objection: ‘Triḥ prathamām anvāha, triḥ uttamām' — here the recital of the ṛk thrice is enjoined; if the ṛk is not an object, then mantra-āvṛtti would have to mean repeated memory of its content, and the primary injunction of repeating the ṛk would be abandoned.

Reply: Therefore, that ātma-caitanya — beginningless and endless, conditioned by mano-vṛtti and abiding in mano-vṛtti — which is what is denoted by the word ‘yajus', is ātma-vijñāna; the mantras (in their essential nature) are this. Thus the eternity of the Vedas is intelligible. Otherwise, if they were external objects like rūpa etc., they would be non-eternal — which is not right. The śruti ‘sarve vedā yatraikaṁ bhavanti, sa mānasīna ātmā' bespeaking unity with the eternal Self, is consistent only on this view of the eternity of ṛk etc. The mantra ‘ṛco akṣare parame vyoman yasmin devā adhi viśve niṣeduḥ' (Śve. Up. 4.8) confirms it.

‘Ādeśa' here is the brāhmaṇa portion — that which prescribes (ādiśati) what is to be enjoined. The mantras and brāhmaṇa seen by Atharvan and Aṅgiras — chiefly devoted to śāntika, pauṣṭika and the like rites of foundation — are the ‘pucchaṁ pratiṣṭhā', because they are predominantly causes of stability. ‘Tad apy eṣa śloko bhavati' — there is also a verse on the manomaya self, as before.
T_C02_S04_V01: From which words turn back along with the mind, unable to attain — knowing the bliss of that Brahman, one fears nothing whatsoever. Of the former (manomaya), this very (vijñānamaya) is the embodied self. From this manomaya self, different and inner, is another self — the vijñānamaya. By it this is filled. He too has the form of a person. Following the form of the former, this is human in form. Of him śraddhā is the head; ṛta the right wing; satya the left wing; yoga the trunk; mahas, the foundation, the tail. Concerning that, there is also this verse:
T_C02_S04_V01::block-0:
Bhāṣya. ‘Yato vāco nivartante, aprāpya manasā saha,' etc. The śārīra ātmā of the former, the prāṇamaya, is this very (manomaya); ‘śārīra' means existing in the body that is prāṇamaya. ‘Tasmād vā etasmāt' as before. ‘Anyo'ntara ātmā vijñānamayaḥ' — different and inner from the manomaya is the vijñānamaya. The manomaya was characterised as the Veda-self. The buddhi, niścayātmaka, applied to the meanings of the Veda, is vijñāna; that is the dharma of the antaḥkaraṇa, of the nature of resolution (adhyavasāya). What is constituted by such niścaya-vijñāna — by the pramāṇa-svarūpas — is the vijñānamaya self. For sacrifice etc. is undertaken on the basis of pramāṇa-vijñāna; the verse will state his being the cause of the yajña.

For one possessed of niścaya-vijñāna, regarding what is to be done, śraddhā arises first; she, being foremost among all duties, is the ‘head' as it were. Ṛta and satya are as already explained. Yoga — yukti, samādhāna — is the ‘ātmā'. For one who is steady (yukta) and concentrated (samāhita), the limbs — śraddhā etc. — become capable of yathārtha apprehension; therefore samādhāna is the ātmā of the vijñānamaya. ‘Mahaḥ' is the mahat-tattva, the first-born — ‘mahad yakṣaṁ prathamajaṁ veda' (Bṛ. Up. 5.4.1) — and is the pucchaṁ pratiṣṭhā because it is the cause; for the cause is the support of effects, as the earth of trees and shrubs. Mahat-tattva is the cause of all vijñānas, hence the support of the vijñānamaya self. ‘Tad apy eṣa śloko bhavati', as before.
T_C02_S05_V01: Vijñāna spreads forth the yajña; it spreads forth the actions too. Vijñāna is what all the gods worship as the eldest Brahman. If one knows Brahman to be Vijñāna, and is not heedless of It, casting off the sins lodged in the body, one obtains all desires. Of the former (manomaya), this very (vijñānamaya) is the embodied self. From this vijñānamaya, different and inner, is another self — the ānandamaya. By it this is filled. He too is in the form of a person. Following the form of the former, this is human in form. Of him priya is the head; moda the right wing; pramoda the left wing; ānanda the trunk; Brahman, the foundation, the tail. Concerning that, there is also this verse:
T_C02_S05_V01::block-0:
Bhāṣya. ‘Vijñānaṁ yajñaṁ tanute' — one possessed of vijñāna spreads forth the yajña, with śraddhā as its preliminary; hence kartṛtva belongs to vijñāna — ‘it spreads forth'. And it ‘spreads forth karmas' too. Since all action is done by one who has vijñāna, it is right that the vijñānamaya self should be Brahman. Further: ‘Vijñānaṁ brahma sarve devāḥ' — Indra and the rest worship vijñāna as the eldest, because it is first-born; or because all vṛttis are preceded by it, hence first-born — that vijñāna-Brahman they worship, with the abhimāna of self upon the vijñānamaya. By such worship of the great Brahman they become possessed of jñāna and aiśvarya.

‘Vijñānaṁ brahma cet veda' — if one not merely ‘knows', but knows it as Brahman; ‘tasmāc cen na pramādyati' — if he does not heedlessly relapse from it. Now, since the self has been imagined upon the external anātmans, there is a danger of pramāda even with respect to the vijñānamaya Brahman. Therefore: ‘tasmāc cen na pramādyati' — abandoning the self-notion in annamaya etc., if one settles in self-identity with the pure vijñānamaya Brahman alone.
