What then? ‘Śarīre pāpmano hitvā' — having cast off in the body itself the sins (pāpmānaḥ) caused by attachment to the body. All sins are rooted in the body-conceit; when, by self-identity with vijñānamaya Brahman, that root is removed, the cessation of sin follows — like the loss of shadow when the umbrella is removed. Therefore, having abandoned in the body itself all sins arising in the body, attaining the form of vijñānamaya Brahman, he obtains, with the very vijñānamaya self, all the kāmas (desires) lodged in him — ‘samaśnute' is to enjoy fully.

The śārīra ātmā of the former (manomaya) is this very (vijñānamaya). ‘Tasmād vā etasmāt' as before.

Now ‘ānandamaya' — that this term means ‘a kārya-self' (an effect-self, not Brahman itself) is to be ascertained from the topic, and from the suffix mayaṬ. The annamaya etc. are bhautika kārya-selves; the topic-set falls within that class — so does this ānandamaya. The mayaṬ here is in the vikāra-sense, as in ‘annamaya'. Hence ānandamaya is to be understood as a kārya-self.

Also from saṅkramaṇa: the text will say ‘ānandamayam ātmānam upasaṅkrāmati'. Saṅkramaṇa is seen of effect-selves (annamaya etc.). The ānandamaya is heard as the karman of saṅkramaṇa, as ‘annamayam ātmānam upasaṅkrāmati'. There can be no upasaṅkramaṇa of the Self by itself, due to ‘adhikāra-virodha' (the topical context against it) and impossibility — for the Self has no internal difference; and Brahman is the very Self of the saṅkramitṛ.

Further, the imagination of head etc. is incompatible (with Brahman): such imagination is not possible upon ākāśādi-causation that is non-effected. From śrutis like ‘adṛśye'nātmye'nirukte'nilayane' (Tai. Up. 2.7.1), ‘asthūlam anaṇu' (Bṛ. Up. 3.8.8), ‘neti neti ātmā' (Bṛ. Up. 3.9.26) — every viśeṣa is denied. The mantra-quotation also fails: in the ānandamaya, perceived directly with priya-head etc., there is no scope for the doubt ‘there is no Brahman' — hence the introductory quotation ‘asann eva sa bhavati asad brahmeti veda cet' (Tai. Up. 2.6.1) would be unintelligible if ānandamaya itself were Brahman. ‘Brahma pucchaṁ pratiṣṭhā' too: if ānandamaya itself were Brahman, the separate mention of Brahman as pratiṣṭhā would be senseless. Hence ānandamaya is a kośa, not Brahman; the ‘brahma' that is the pucchaṁ pratiṣṭhā is the very Brahman to be reached.
T_C02_S06_V01: Asat indeed he becomes who knows Brahman as asat (non-existent); but he who knows ‘Brahman is' — him do they know as existing. The śārīra-self of the former (vijñānamaya) is this very (ānandamaya). Now hence the anu-praśnas: ‘Does even the unknower, departing hence, attain that world? Or rather, does the knower, departing hence, attain that world?' — He desired: ‘May I be many; let me be born forth.' He performed tapas. Having performed tapas, He created all this — whatever there is. Having created it, He entered into it. Having entered, He became the sat and the tyat, the niruktam and the anirukta, the niḷayana and the aniḷayana, the vijñāna and the avijñāna, the satya and the anṛta — all this became satya. ‘That is satya', so they declare. Concerning that there is also this verse:
T_C02_S06_V01::block-0:
Bhāṣya. ‘Asann eva sa bhavati' — like that which is asat (non-existent — like a hare's horn — and so unrelated to puruṣārtha), so does he become — unrelated to puruṣārtha. Who? He who knows Brahman as asat — non-existent. By contrast, what is the seat of all alternatives, the seed of all activity, transcending every viśeṣa, yet ‘exists' — he who knows Brahman as ‘sat'. Why this doubt about the existence of Brahman? Because Brahman lies beyond vyavahāra. The buddhi, conditioned by ‘existence' only with respect to the vyavahāra-domain (mere ‘vāc-ārambhaṇa'), supposes that what lies outside vyavahāra must be non-existent — as a pot is sat being object of vyavahāra, while the contrary is asat. By this similarity, doubt of Brahman's non-existence might arise. Therefore: ‘asti brahmeti ced veda'.

What then is the result for him who knows Brahman as ‘sat'? Brahmavids know him to be ‘sat' — existing in the form of Brahman, having gained the supreme reality as his own self. From his apprehension of ‘sat' he is acknowledged by other knowers of Brahman as one indeed worthy to be known like Brahman. Or alternatively: he who thinks Brahman is non-existent denies the entire ‘sat-mārga' — the order of varṇa, āśrama, and dharma — for that order is intended for brahma-prāpti. Hence in the world he is called nāstika, asat (sinful). The opposite — he who thinks ‘Brahman is' — having faith, takes up the sat-mārga of varṇa-āśrama, the means to brahma-prāpti; therefore the good (sādhus) recognise him as ‘sat', a worker on the path of the good. Hence: ‘Brahman is to be known as existing.'

The śārīra ātmā of the previous (vijñānamaya) — dwelling in the vijñānamaya body — is this very (ānandamaya). Of him there is no doubt of non-existence (since he is directly experienced as priya, moda, pramoda etc.); but as regards Brahman, all viśeṣas being repelled, the doubt of non-existence is reasonable, since Brahman is at parity with all things. Hence ‘ataḥ' — therefore — the ‘anu-praśnas' of the listening pupil now follow upon the ācārya's pronouncement. The plural ‘anu-praśnas' indicates more than one. Brahman as universal cause, the ākāśādi-cause, is common to vidvān and avidvān; hence one even fears that the avidvān too might attain Brahman. Hence the question: ‘Uta avidvān amuṁ lokaṁ pretya kaścana gacchati?' (the word ‘cana' carries the sense of ‘even') — does even the unknower attain? And as a second question of the same type: ‘or does he not attain?' To the knower, two further questions: if even the avidvān reaches the common cause, then doubt about the vidvān's attaining arises; conversely, if the avidvān does not reach Brahman the universal cause, doubt about the vidvān reaching arises. Hence: ‘āho vidvān…' By the sandhi-procedure (taking ‘u' from below and ‘t' from the previous ‘uta', and prefixing ‘uta' to ‘āho'), it is read ‘ut-āho vidvān…' — ‘either the vidvān, departing from here, attains that loka' or, like the avidvān, does not attain — these are the two questions of this set.
T_C02_S06_V01::block-1:
Bhāṣya. The reply: the answer-section now begins. There ‘existence' (astitva) is first established. As to ‘satyaṁ jñānam anantaṁ brahma' — what makes Brahman ‘satya' has to be set forth. By stating its sattva, satyatva is being stated; for ‘sad eva satyam' — by śruti's avadhāraṇa, satya is identical with sat. How is this the import of this whole section? By the words. The subsequent sentences are joined by this very meaning — ‘tat satyam ity ācakṣate' (Tai. Up. 2.6.1), ‘yad eṣa ākāśa ānando na syāt' (Tai. Up. 2.7.1) and the rest.

Now there might be the doubt: ‘Brahman is asat'. Why? Because what is sat is grasped specifically (viśeṣataḥ) — like a pot. What is asat is not perceived — like a hare's horn. Brahman is not perceived in such a way; therefore by aviśeṣa-grahaṇa it is asat.

Reply: No — because Brahman is the cause of ākāśa etc. Brahman is not non-existent. Why? Because all kāryas — ākāśa etc. — are seen as born from Brahman. Whatever is born from a thing implies that thing's existence — like clay or seed for a pot or sprout. Hence Brahman exists. Nothing in the world is born from asat. If nāma-rūpa-kārya were born from asat, being self-less it would not be perceived; but it is perceived. Therefore Brahman is. If asat were the cause, the kārya would itself partake of asat-character — but it does not. Hence Brahman exists. The other śruti — ‘kutha asataḥ saj jāyeta' (Chā. Up. 6.2.2) — by reasoning shows the impossibility of the birth of sat from asat. Therefore ‘Brahman is sat'.

Objection: If Brahman, like clay or seed, is the cause, then it would be acetana.

Reply: No — because of its kāmayitṛtva (being an agent of desire). No acetana being is found to ‘desire'. Brahman has been declared sarvajña; hence kāmayitṛtva is intelligible.

Objection: If it desires, like us, it must be ‘unfulfilled in desire' (anāpta-kāma).

Reply: No — because of its svātantrya. As in others, kāma operates by overpowering them; not so in Brahman. Brahman's kāmas are pure, of the nature of satya-jñāna, identical with His own self. They do not impel Brahman; rather Brahman impels them with regard to creatures' karma. Hence Brahman is svatantra in respect of kāma; hence not anāpta-kāma. Also, no need of other instruments — others' kāmas depend on adṛṣṭa, instruments etc. external to themselves; not so Brahman's. Brahman's kāmas are non-different from His own self.

Thus: ‘So'kāmayata' — that ātmā from whom ākāśa was born desired. How? ‘Bahu syām' — let me become many. How can the One become many without entering into another? The answer: ‘Prajāyeya' — let me be born forth — not in the sense of producing a son of separate substance, but by the manifestation of ātma-stha, hitherto unmanifest, nāma-rūpa. When the latent nāma-rūpa, abiding in the Self, are made manifest, then — without abandoning Brahman's own form — they are made manifest, undivided in space and time from Brahman, in all states. That very nāma-rūpa-vyākaraṇa is Brahman's bahu-bhavana. There is no other way for a partless Brahman to become many or few — any other view (as if Brahman were like an elephant moving here and there) would contradict everything.
T_C02_S06_V01::block-2:
Bhāṣya. Here arises the inquiry: how did He enter? The creator — did He enter in His own form, or in some other? Which is right? Since the past gerund ‘kṛtvā' is heard, the same Creator must be the enterer.

Objection: If Brahman is the cause like clay, then the kārya is of the nature of the cause — clay itself becomes pot in the form of pot. Hence after generation of the kārya, no separate ‘entering' of the cause is reasonable, since clay's entry into the pot is only its modification as pot. If you say: just as clay enters the pot in the form of powder, so the Self enters the kārya as nāma-rūpa — and śruti corroborates: ‘with this jīva-self I will enter' (Chā. Up. 6.3.2) — this too is not right, because of the unity of Brahman. Clay being many and possessed of parts, its entry as powder makes sense; but Brahman being one and partless, no such entry is possible. How then is entry?

Reply: But entry is heard: ‘tad evānuprāviśat'. It must therefore be a real entry. If you propose Brahman is sa-avayava, like the hand entering the mouth, jīvātma-prāveśa would be intelligible — No: there is no place that is ātma-śūnya into which Brahman could enter. There is no place outside the kārya — for Brahman has parinated into kārya. If the cause re-enters, it would lose its jīvātmatva, like the pot losing its potness on entering clay. The śruti ‘tad evānuprāviśat' would also fail.

Nor can it mean Brahman becomes another effect: a pot does not become another pot, and the śruti distinguishing jīva from nāma-rūpa-kārya would be violated. If this were so, there would be no mokṣa — for one is not freed from oneself by becoming what one is.

Nor by ‘parinated as outer-and-inner' — the cause-Brahman as outer-form (śarīrādhāra), and as inner-jīva-form (ādheya): No — because that which is inside cannot be said to ‘enter' it. Entry is from without — as ‘having built a house, he entered'. Nor as pratibimba in water (jala-sūryaka): Brahman is not paricchinna or mūrta; only the bounded-figured can have such a reflection — and there is no other place outside Brahman with a reflective medium. Hence pratibimba-praveśa is not right.

Then, no entry at all? But śruti is the means of knowledge in atīndriya matters, and one cannot dismiss it. Yet if no entry, the verse becomes purposeless…
T_C02_S06_V01::block-3:
Bhāṣya. Reply: Having created this kārya — ākāśa etc. — He, as it were, having entered into it, is perceived in the heart-cave (guhā), in the buddhi, as draṣṭṛ, śrotṛ, mantṛ, vijñātṛ — endowed with these viśeṣas. That itself is His ‘entry'. Therefore Brahman, the cause, exists; from existence, ‘is' alone is to be apprehended. Having entered the kārya, what? ‘Sac ca tyac ca abhavat' — He became sat (mūrta, gross) and tyat (amūrta, subtle). The mūrta and amūrta — the unmanifest nāma-rūpas in the Self — were manifested by the entered Self, called by the words sat and tyat; but since they are non-divided in space-time from the Self, the Self is said to ‘become' them.

Further: ‘niruktaṁ ca aniruktaṁ ca'. ‘Niruktam' is what is set apart from like and unlike, marked by definite place-time, called ‘this-that'; ‘aniruktam' is its opposite. Both qualify mūrta and amūrta respectively. Like ‘sac ca tyac ca' (perceptible vs imperceptible), so ‘niḷayana' (abode — a property of the mūrta) and ‘aniḷayana' (its opposite — of the amūrta). ‘Tyat-anirukta-aniḷayana' too, though properties of the amūrta, refer to the manifested domain — being heard as sarga-uttara-kāla-bhāva. ‘Tyat' here means prāṇādi anirukta-aniḷayana — hence properties of amūrta-vyākṛta.

‘Vijñānam' is the cetana; ‘avijñānam' its absence — pāṣāṇa etc. ‘Satyam' — vyavahāra-domain, not paramārtha-satya. Only one paramārtha-satya is Brahman. Here it is relative satya — water relative to mirage being satya, etc. ‘Anṛtam' is the contrary. What more? All this — the mūrta-amūrta-dharma-jāta — became sat — paramārtha-satya — what is paramārtha-satya? Brahman, ‘satyaṁ jñānam anantam' from the topic. Since sat-tyat-niḷayana etc. — every nāma-rūpa-vikāra, denoted by ‘sat' — became Brahman, beyond which no nāma-rūpa-vikāra exists; hence brahmavids declare ‘That is satya'.

The ‘asti-nāsti' anu-praśna being the topic: in the answer-section it has been said ‘ātmākāmayata bahu syām'. Having created kārya — ākāśa etc., sat-tyat-marked — and having entered it, seeing, hearing, thinking, knowing, He became many. Hence this very ākāśādi-cause, abiding within the kārya, in the heart-cave (parame vyoman), perceived as that very pratyaya-avabhāsa, exists — so should one know. ‘Tad apy eṣa śloko bhavati' — as the verses revealed the annamaya etc. earlier, so this verse manifests the existence of the inmost ātman through the kārya.
T_C02_S07_V01: Asat verily was this in the beginning. From it, indeed, sat was born. That made of itself its own self; therefore it is called sukṛta. That which is sukṛta — He, verily, is rasa. Having gained this rasa alone, one becomes blissful. For who could breathe in, who could breathe out, were this bliss not in the ākāśa? It is He, indeed, who delights. When this seeker finds in this Adṛśya, Anātmya, Anirukta, Aniḷayana, fearless support, then he attains fearlessness. But when he makes any small distinction in That, then fear arises for him. For the knower who reflects not aright, that very (Brahman) becomes fear. Concerning that there is also this verse:
T_C02_S07_V01::block-0:
Bhāṣya. ‘Asad vā idam agra āsīt'. ‘Asat' here means the avyākṛta — Brahman before the differentiation of nāma-rūpa-viśeṣas — not absolutely non-existent, for from absolute asat no sat is born. ‘Idam' is the nāma-rūpa-viśiṣṭa, vyākṛta jagat. ‘Agre' — before, prior to its production. Brahman alone, denoted as ‘asat', was. From that asat, vai, sat — with differentiated nāma-rūpa — was born. Was the kārya separated from it, like a son from a father? No. ‘Tad ātmānaṁ svayam akuruta' — that asat-named (Brahman) made its own Self by itself. Therefore Brahman is called ‘sukṛta' — self-doer (svayaṁ-kartṛ); for as the cause of all, Brahman is famed in the world as ‘sva-yaṁ kartṛ'. Or: since by itself it has done everything, by being also of the form of puṇya, it is sukṛta. In any case, the worldly fame of ‘sukṛta' as the cause of fruit-relationship — whether puṇya or other — is intelligible only when there is an eternal cetana cause; hence Brahman exists, by the very repute of sukṛta.

Further, Brahman exists because it is rasa. Whence the rasatva of Brahman? ‘Yad vai tat sukṛtaṁ raso vai saḥ.' ‘Rasa' — that which is the cause of contentment, the bringer of bliss — sweet, sour and the like — is well known in the world. Having obtained the rasa, this man becomes ānandī, blissful. No one is seen made happy by asat. Even brāhmaṇas without external rasa-means, anīhā (without striving), nireṣaṇa (without longing), are seen full of bliss as if from the gain of an external rasa — surely Brahman alone is rasa for them. Hence Brahman, the cause of their bliss, exists, and is rasavat.

Further, Brahman exists because of the visible activities of prāṇa etc. This piṇḍa breathes in by prāṇa, breathes out by apāna; thus the vāyu-natured and indriya-natured activities are accomplished by the body-organ aggregate. Such an aggregate — coordinated to one purpose — is impossible without a non-aggregate cetana, since nowhere else is such found. Therefore: ‘Yad eṣa ākāśa ānando na syāt' — if this ānanda lodged in the supreme ākāśa-cave were not, who would carry on the apāna activity? Who would breathe in? Hence Brahman exists, for whose sake all bodily-organ-prāṇana-activities are. And the bliss of the world is caused by Him: ‘eṣa hy evānandayāti' — He, the supreme ātman, makes the world blissful in proportion to dharma. The Self, of the form of bliss, is, by avidyā, perceived as paricchinna by living beings.

Brahman is also bhayābhaya-hetu (cause of fear and fearlessness) for the avidvān and the vidvān respectively. By recourse to a sat-vastu, fearlessness arises; by recourse to asat-vastu, fearlessness is impossible. How is Brahman the cause of abhaya? ‘Yadā hy eva eṣa etasmin' — when the seeker finds in this Brahman — what kind? ‘Adṛśye': dṛśya is what is seen, the modification (vikāra), since vikāra is meant for being seen; ‘adṛśya' — what is not seen, i.e., a-vikāra. ‘Anātmya' — not bodily, since it is non-vikāra; ‘anirukta' — what cannot be specifically defined, since viśeṣa-niruktī is for vikāras; Brahman is a-vikāra, the cause of all vikāras; hence ‘anirukta'. From this, ‘anilayana' — without a niḷayana (abode-form, a property of the mūrta only)…
T_C02_S08_V01: Out of fear of Him the wind blows. Out of fear the sun rises. Out of fear of Him fire and Indra (function), and death, the fifth, runs. This now is an investigation into bliss. Suppose there be a youth — a noble youth, well-versed in the Veda, most ready (in command), firmest (of resolve), strongest (of body); and that this whole earth, full of wealth, were his. That is one human bliss. Whatever are a hundred such human blisses —
T_C02_S08_V02: — that is one bliss of the human-gandharvas, and (likewise) of the śrotriya untouched by desire. Whatever are a hundred such blisses of the human-gandharvas, that is one bliss of the deva-gandharvas, and of the śrotriya untouched by desire. Whatever are a hundred such blisses of the deva-gandharvas, that is one bliss of the pitṛs whose worlds are long-enduring, and of the śrotriya untouched by desire. Whatever are a hundred such blisses of these pitṛs, that is one bliss of the gods who are gods by birth (in the deva-loka).
T_C02_S08_V03: And this is the bliss of the śrotriya untouched by desire. Whatever are a hundred such blisses of the gods born in the deva-loka — that is one bliss of the karma-devas, who attain godhood by (Vedic) action; and of the śrotriya untouched by desire. Whatever are a hundred such blisses of the karma-devas — that is one bliss of the (thirty-three) gods (themselves), and of the śrotriya untouched by desire. Whatever are a hundred such blisses of the gods — that is one bliss of Indra.
T_C02_S08_V04: And of the śrotriya untouched by desire. Whatever are a hundred such blisses of Indra — that is one bliss of Bṛhaspati, and of the śrotriya untouched by desire. Whatever are a hundred such blisses of Bṛhaspati — that is one bliss of Prajāpati, and of the śrotriya untouched by desire. Whatever are a hundred such blisses of Prajāpati — that is one bliss of Brahmā (Hiraṇyagarbha), and of the śrotriya untouched by desire.
T_C02_S08_V04::block-0:
"Out of fear (bhīṣā) — that is, through dread of Him — the wind blows. Out of fear the sun rises. Out of fear of Him fire and Indra (function); and death, the fifth, runs." — for the wind and the rest, though great and themselves lordly powers, are nevertheless held to their respective tasks of blowing and so on, tasks heavy with effort, in unfailing regularity. Such regularity is intelligible only when there is a Ruler who governs them. Since their activity is constrained by law, there must exist a cause of fear for them — a Ruler who is Brahman. Inasmuch as they, like servants under a king, function out of fear of this Brahman, that very cause of their fear is the blissful Brahman.

Of this Brahman, then — of this very ānanda — there now follows an investigation (mīmāṃsā), a deliberate inquiry. "What is there to investigate concerning bliss?" The reply: Is bliss something produced by the relation between subject and object, like the worldly pleasures of men, or is it natural and intrinsic? Such is the inquiry into ānanda.
T_C02_S08_V04::block-1:
Now, worldly bliss — caused by the convergence of outer and inner means — has its highest grade. It is precisely such bliss that is here singled out, in order to lead the mind step by step toward the bliss of Brahman; for it is by means of this familiar bliss that the bliss accessible only when the consciousness has been turned away from objects can itself be approached. Even worldly bliss is but a particle (mātrā) of the bliss of Brahman: when the inner Knowledge is veiled by avidyā and that avidyā waxes strong, the bliss of Brahman gets refracted — through the agency of beings from Brahmā downwards, in proportion to their karma, to the measure of their knowledge, and to the contact with objects and instruments — and so appears in the world as the unsteady, fluctuating worldly bliss.

This very bliss, when avidyā, desire, and karma are progressively diminished, comes to be experienced — directly perceived by the wise śrotriya untouched by desire — at successively higher stations: the human, the human-gandharva, and so on, with a hundred-fold increase at each step, all the way up to the bliss of Hiraṇyagarbha-Brahmā.
T_C02_S08_V04::block-2:
But when the division of subject and object — itself the work of avidyā — is altogether dissolved, then through vidyā the natural, full, one, non-dual bliss alone remains. With a view to bringing this out, the text goes on:

"yuvā" — one in his first prime; "sādhu-yuvā" — sādhu and yuvā taken together qualify the youth: one may be young yet not noble, or noble yet not young; hence the qualification — "let him be a sādhu-yuvā." "Adhyāyaka" — one who has studied the Veda. "Āśiṣṭha" — most ready (in command). "Dṛḍhiṣṭha" — firmest (of resolve). "Baliṣṭha" — strongest (of body). Thus he is endowed with all inner means. "Tasyeyaṃ pṛthivī sarvā vittasya pūrṇā" — and let this whole wide earth be his, replete with wealth, that is, with the means of enjoyment seen and unseen and with the means for ritual action — meaning, let him be sovereign of the earth. The bliss of such a man — that is one human bliss, the highest among men.

"Hundredfold this human bliss is one bliss of the human-gandharvas" — meaning, the bliss of the human-gandharvas exceeds the human a hundred times. The human-gandharvas are men who, by special karma and special knowledge, have attained gandharva-hood. Possessed of powers such as becoming invisible, with bodies and organs of subtle quality, they suffer little obstruction; they have the means to ward off the pairs of opposites. Hence in the human-gandharva, unobstructed and equipped with such defences, there arises a special tranquillity of mind (citta-prasāda); and from such special tranquillity, special manifestation of pleasure follows. In this manner, by ever-finer mental tranquillity, the hundred-fold increase of bliss at each successive plane is intelligible.

The addition of "akāmahata" already at the very first stage is meant to indicate this: the śrotriya who is unsmitten by craving for human objects of enjoyment must himself be reckoned to enjoy a bliss a hundred-fold above the merely human — equal to that of the human-gandharva. "Sādhu-yuvā adhyāyaka" gives, by implication, the conditions of being a śrotriya and being free from sin — for these two are required uniformly throughout. "Akāmahatatva," however, varies in degree according to the rise or fall of objective enjoyments, and accordingly varies the degree of pleasure. Hence the explicit mention of akāmahatatva: by its varying degrees the hundred-fold rise of bliss is established, and thereby its character as a means to the supreme ānanda is taught.

The rest has been explained. "Deva-gandharvas" are gandharvas by birth as such. "Cira-loka-loka" qualifies the pitṛs — those whose world endures long. "Ājāna" is the deva-loka; those born there by virtue of smārta works are the ājāna-jas. The karma-devas are those who attain to the gods through purely Vedic action such as agnihotra. The "devas" proper are the thirty-three eaters of oblation; Indra is their lord; Bṛhaspati is his teacher. Prajāpati is Virāj — Brahmā with the three worlds as his body, the totality and the individual together, pervading the whole circle of saṃsāra. And there, where all these grades of bliss converge into oneness, where dharma — the cause of bliss — and knowledge — its content — and akāmahatatva all reach their unsurpassed limit, there stands Hiraṇyagarbha-Brahmā; his bliss it is that the śrotriya, sinless and free from craving, perceives directly on every side.

From this it is to be understood that there are these three means (śrotriyatva, avṛjinatva, akāmahatatva). Among them, śrotriyatva and avṛjinatva are taken as fixed, while akāmahatatva is what is graded; hence the latter is to be recognized as the principal means. The bliss of Brahmā — accessible to the śrotriya in proportion to his akāmahatatva — is itself but a particle, a single region, of the supreme ānanda, as another text declares: "upon a particle of this very bliss other beings live" — [śloka quoted in the text].
T_C02_S08_V05: He who is here in man, and He who is there in the sun — He is one. He who knows thus, on departing from this world, attains unto this Self made of food; attains unto this Self made of vital breath; attains unto this Self made of mind; attains unto this Self made of cognition; attains unto this Self made of bliss. On this, too, there is this verse:
T_C02_S08_V05::block-0: Now the fruit of this mīmāṃsā is summed up:
T_C02_S08_V05::block-1:
"He who is here in man." — He who, hidden in the cave, in the highest space, having created the entire effect from ākāśa down to the food-sheath, then entered into it — He is the one being indicated. Who is this? "He who is here in man." "And He who is there in the sun" — that supreme bliss, perceived directly by the śrotriya, of whose single region Brahmā and the rest of beings live their pleasure-allotted lives — He is the one indicated by "yaścāsāvāditye." "Sa ekaḥ" — He is one, just as the spaces in different jars and the universal space are one.

Objection: When designating Him, why is it not enough to say "He who is here in man" — i.e., simply within the body — without further specification? Why also bring in the sun? Indeed "He who is here in the right eye" would be apt, since that is a familiar designation.

Reply: No, because the topic is the supreme. Throughout this section the supreme Ātman is the topic — "in the unseen, the bodiless" (Tai. 2.7), "out of fear of Him the wind blows" (Tai. 2.8), "this is the investigation of bliss" (Tai. 2.8). It is not proper, all of a sudden, to introduce something not under discussion. Moreover, the knowledge of the supreme Self is what is intended. Therefore it is the supreme alone that is designated as "sa ekaḥ."

But, you say, the topic was the investigation of bliss; its conclusion too should be summed up. — That is precisely what is done: the natural, undivided bliss is the supreme Ātman Himself, not anything generated by the relation of subject and object. And the very mode of statement matches this: "He who is here in man, and He who is there in the sun — He is one" — by setting aside the particular features that arise from being lodged in different seats. Even so, what is the use of mentioning the sun in particular? — It is not useless: it is mentioned in order to set aside both "more" and "less." Within duality, the highest grade of duality is that within the body of the sun, including both gross (mūrta) and subtle (amūrta) forms; if even that supreme grade, when the differences attaching to the puruṣa-form are dissolved away, becomes equal to the supreme bliss, then for one who has reached that state there is neither any "higher" nor "lower" — and thus he attains "fearlessness, the firm ground."
T_C02_S08_V05::block-2: The supplementary questions, "Is it? Is it not?" have been explained. By the considerations of the production of effects, the gaining of essence, the act of breathing, fearlessness in the wise, and the seeing of fear (in the ignorant), the very first supplementary — whether the cause of ākāśa and the rest is or is not — has been answered: it is. Two further supplementaries concerned the wise man's attainment, and the ignorant man's non-attainment, of Brahman; of these, the last ("does the wise man attain or not?") is the one now to be addressed. By that very answer the middle question is also disposed of; so it is not separately taken up. — "Sa yaḥ kaścit evam vit" — whoever knows thus, that is, knows the Brahman as just expounded — knows it as setting aside both excess and defect, as non-dual, as 'I am Existence-Knowledge-Infinite' — he is "evaṃ-vit"; the word "evam" referring back to the topic just expounded. Of him what? "Departing from this world" — for this world is the entire complex of seen and unseen objects of desire; from this world he turns away, becomes wholly unconcerned, and "attains unto this Self made of food, as expounded" — i.e., he sees no aggregate of objects as separate from the food-made bodily Ātman; he sees all the gross elements as the food-made Self. Then, more inward, he attains the Self made of breath, which abides within the food-Self yet is not separated from it; and so the mind-made, the cognition-made, and the bliss-made. Then "in the unseen, the bodiless, the unutterable, the without-abode, he finds fearlessness, the firm ground."
T_C02_S08_V05::block-3:
Here a question for reflection arises. Who is this "evaṃ-vit," and how does he so attain? Is the agent of attainment someone other than, and divided from, the supreme Self? Or is he the very same?

[Pūrvapakṣa]: What does it matter? — If he is other, the śrutis are violated: "Having created it, He entered into it" (Tai. 2.6); "He thinks, 'this is other than me, I am other than that' — he does not know" (Bṛ. 1.4.10); "One only, without a second" (Chā. 6.2.1); "That thou art" (Chā. 6.8.16). On the other hand, if the very supreme Self attains the bliss-made Self, the relation of agent and act fails. And the supreme would either become saṃsārin or cease to be supreme. If on either alternative the difficulty is unavoidable, this inquiry is in vain. — But if on one of the alternatives, or on a third undefective alternative, the difficulty does not arise, that is the meaning of the śāstra; and so the inquiry is again in vain.

[Siddhāntin]: No — the inquiry is precisely for fixing which alternative holds. True, were the difficulty unsolvable on either side, or were a third alternative already ascertained as defectless, the inquiry would be idle; but no such ascertainment has yet been made; hence the inquiry is meaningful.

[Objection]: But you may inquire and yet fail to settle. Will you say the Vedic word does not need to be settled? — Indeed I will. Why your doubt? — Because of the multitude of opponents: you uphold non-duality and stand by the meaning of the Veda, but the many vādins of duality, outside the Veda, oppose you. — That very fact is my blessing — that you set me as a single yogin against many opponent yogins. So I shall conquer them all. I therefore commence the reflection.
T_C02_S08_V05::block-4:
[Siddhānta]: Indeed it is the same Self alone, since the very being-as-That is what is intended. By the knowledge of That, the supreme-Self-being is here intended — "the knower of Brahman attains the Highest." For one thing cannot become another. — Objection: Even for the same Self, becoming-That is unintelligible. — Reply: No; for it is intended to dispel the non-Self superimposed by avidyā. The attainment of one's own Self that is taught by Brahma-vidyā is for the sake of removing the not-Self — namely, the food-and-the-rest particular forms — superimposed by avidyā as if they were the Self. — How is this purport made out? — From the fact that what is taught is bare vidyā; and the observed fruit of vidyā is the cessation of avidyā. Here, in the means to Self-attainment, vidyā alone is taught.

[Objection]: As when one is given knowledge of the road to a place, the knowledge is a means to attainment; the same here. — Reply: Where the very means to becoming the Self is mere knowledge, this analogy fails. Why? — In the case of reaching another country, one teaches knowledge of the road, not knowledge of the village itself; one does not say "the village is the goer." But here, apart from Brahma-vidyā, no other knowledge of any other means is taught. — Objection: Brahma-vidyā, supported by karma and other auxiliaries, is a means to attaining the Supreme. — Reply: No; this has been already refuted by the earlier statement that liberation is eternal (and hence not produced by any combined means). Moreover the śruti, "Having created it, He entered into it," shows that the effect is itself That-Self.

And this is required by the doctrine of fearlessness as firm ground. For if the wise man saw something other than his own Self, then "he finds fearlessness" would not hold — there being no other supreme thing as a possible cause of fear. And if such other is the work of avidyā, it is intelligible that, by vidyā, it should be seen as no real thing — just as a second moon is unreal, since it is not perceived by a sound eye. — Objection: But it is perceived. — Reply: No; in deep sleep and in samādhi it is not perceived. — Objection: In deep sleep the non-perception is like that of one whose mind is engaged elsewhere. — Reply: No; for nothing whatever is then perceived. — Objection: In waking and dream other things are perceived, hence they exist. — Reply: No; the perceiving of "other" in waking and dream is itself the work of avidyā; in the absence of avidyā it does not occur. — Objection: The non-perception in deep sleep is also the work of avidyā. — Reply: No; for it is natural. The very nature (tattva) of a thing is its non-modification, since it does not depend on anything else. Modification is not the nature, since it depends on something else. The nature of a thing is not relative to operative factors; difference is relative to factors, and difference is modification. The perception of "other" in waking and dream is just such a difference. Whatever is the form of a thing not dependent on anything else, that is its nature; what is dependent on another is not its nature, for in the absence of that other it ceases. Hence, by being natural, deep sleep is not a 'difference' as waking and dream are.

For those, on the other hand, who hold that Īśvara is other than the self and the effect is other again, fear cannot be uprooted, since fear has its cause in another; and the loss of an other that exists is impossible; nor can a non-existent other be acquired. — Objection: That other, when joined with relations, becomes the cause of fear. — Reply: No; the same difficulty arises again: even of that auxiliary-helped 'other' — eternal or non-eternal — taken as cause of fear, the impossibility of its destruction equally prevents the cessation of fear; or if one allowed its destruction, then the existent and non-existent would interchange, and there would be no rest anywhere. On the doctrine of oneness, however, fear with its causes [is consumed by knowledge].
T_C02_S09_V01: From which words turn back, together with mind, not having reached — knowing the bliss of Brahman, one fears not from any quarter. Such a one is not tormented by the thought, "Why have I not done good? Why have I done evil?" The one who knows thus saves himself from these (two thoughts); for he saves himself indeed from both as Self, who knows thus. Such is the upaniṣad.
T_C02_S09_V01::block-0:
"Yataḥ" — from which Self, of the character previously described, the non-dual, free from determinations (nirvikalpa), and bliss; "vācaḥ" — words, that is, designations whose objects are determinate things such as substance and the rest, employed by speakers, by way of generality of being, even with respect to the non-determinate, non-dual Brahman, in order to disclose Him; "aprāpya" — without reaching, without illuminating; "nivartante" — they turn back, that is, they desist of their own incapacity. "Manas" means cognition (pratyaya). Cognition operates wherever a designation operates, even with regard to a thing beyond the senses, and turns toward that object for its disclosure. Where there is cognition, there is operation of words. Hence everywhere speech and mind, designation and cognition, operate together. Therefore, words used by speakers in every way to disclose Brahman — when their object is one not falling within cognition, beyond designation, beyond seeing, and so qualified — turn back together with the mind, the cognition that is competent to disclose all things.

Knowing such bliss of Brahman — of one who is a śrotriya, sinless, untouched by craving, freed from every desire — bliss that is the very Self, free from the relation of subject and object, natural, eternal, undivided, the supreme ānanda — knowing it, in the manner stated, "na bibheti kutaścana" — he fears nothing from any quarter, for there is no occasion (nimitta). For him, the wise, there exists no other separate thing whence fear could arise. Only when, by avidyā, one makes an inner gap between (Self and object), does fear arise — that alone is intelligible. But for the wise, since the work of avidyā has perished — like the second moon seen by one with diseased vision — there is no cause of fear: hence "he fears nothing from any quarter" is well established.

In the section on the manomaya, a mantra was likewise quoted, since the mind is the means of the knowledge of Brahman. There, Brahman-hood was superimposed upon the mind by way of upāsanā, and to praise it, mere fear was negated by "he never fears." Here, however, in the context of non-duality, what is negated is the very cause of fear: "he fears nothing from any quarter."

[Objection]: But are there not causes of fear — failure to do good, and the doing of evil? — Reply: Not so. How? — "Etam ha vāva," with the two emphatic particles, "na tapati" — does not torment, does not agitate, does not afflict him. How is it that omission of the good and commission of the evil do not torment him? — "Why did I not do that good, fine deed?" — such after-burning arises in the ignorant when death draws near. Likewise, "Why did I do that evil, prohibited deed?" — such torment arises from fear of falling into hell and other sufferings. These two — failure to do good and commission of evil — though they torment the ignorant, do not torment him so. Why not the wise? — Because such a knower sees both these — the not-doing-of-good and the doing-of-evil, the causes of torment — within himself, that is, sees them as the supreme Ātman; "ātmānaṃ spṛṇute" — he gladdens, or strengthens, his Self. For such a wise one, having reduced both puṇya and pāpa to the form of Self alone, deprived of their distinct characters, he saves his Self alone (from them).

Who? — "Ya evaṃ veda" — he who thus knows the non-dual, ānanda Brahman, as expounded. For one whose puṇya and pāpa have been seen as Self, they become impotent, non-tormenting, and unable to start a fresh birth. Such, then, in this Vallī, is the upaniṣad of Brahma-vidyā as expounded — meaning, the supreme secret among all vidyās is here disclosed; the highest good rests in this.
T_C03_S01_V00: Om. May He protect us both. May He nourish us both. May we both work with vigour. May our study be effulgent. May we not hate one another. Om. Peace, peace, peace.
T_C03_S01_V01: Bhṛgu, indeed, the son of Varuṇa, approached his father Varuṇa, saying: "Sir, teach me Brahman." To him he declared this: "Food, breath, eye, ear, mind, speech." To him he then said: "That from which these beings are born, that by which, when born, they live, that towards which, departing, they enter — that seek to know. That is Brahman." He performed tapas. Having performed tapas —
T_C03_S01_V01::block-0: Brahman, which is Truth, Knowledge, Infinite, having created the entire effect — from ākāśa down to the food-sheath — and having entered into it so as to be apprehended, as it were, with particulars, is yet from all those effects distinct, possessed of qualities such as invisibility, etc., bliss only; therefore: "He am I" — thus must one know, since the very purpose of the entry is just this. For one who knows thus, neither auspicious nor inauspicious karma initiates a fresh birth — such is the intended meaning of the Ānanda-vallī. And so Brahma-vidyā stands concluded. Now, beyond this, the tapas which is the means to Brahma-vidyā has to be expounded; and the upāsanās concerning food and the rest have not yet been treated. Hence the present section is begun:
T_C03_S01_V01::block-1:
The narrative is by way of praising the vidyā: it has been told by a father to his beloved son. "Bhṛguḥ vai vāruṇiḥ." — The particle "vai" recalls something well-known; one called Bhṛgu, well-known by name, is being recalled. "Vāruṇiḥ" — the offspring of Varuṇa is vāruṇi. He, desirous of knowing Brahman, approached his father Varuṇa with the mantra "Adhīhi bhagavo Brahma" — "teach me, expound to me, Brahman." The father, to that son who had approached duly, declared this saying: "food, breath, eye, ear, mind, speech." Annam — the body, with its inwardness; prāṇa — the eater, the prāṇa; thereafter the means of cognition — eye, ear, mind, speech — these he declared as the doors to the apprehension of Brahman.

Having stated these doors — food and the rest — he went on to tell Bhṛgu the laksaṇa of Brahman. What is it? — "That from which (yataḥ) these beings, beginning with Brahmā and ending with the clump of grass, are born; that by which, when born, they live, hold their breaths, grow; and that into which, at the time of dissolution, they go, into which they enter (abhisaṃviśanti), reaching identity with which itself; that, the very Self of which the beings do not abandon throughout origination, sustenance, and dissolution — that is the lakṣaṇa of Brahman. That Brahman seek to know specifically (vijijñāsasva)" — that is, through the doorway of food and the rest, attain the Brahman of such a description.

Another śruti — "the Prāṇa of prāṇa, the Eye of eye, the Ear of ear, the Food of food, the Mind of mind: those who know — they have realized the ancient, primal Brahman" (Bṛ. 4.4.18) — likewise shows that these are the doors to the apprehension of Brahman.

That Bhṛgu, having heard from his father the doors of Brahman-apprehension and the lakṣaṇa, performed tapas, since tapas is a means to Brahman-apprehension. — Whence, then, did Bhṛgu come to take tapas — though not enjoined by his father — as the means? — Because of the partial nature of his father's statement. The lakṣaṇa, the door, were stated, but not Brahman directly. Otherwise the father would have indicated Brahman in its very own form to his inquisitive son: "such-and-such is Brahman"; he did not so designate it, but spoke only with a residue. So Bhṛgu understood: surely the father expects something more for the knowledge of Brahman.

The choice of tapas in particular: tapas is the most powerful of all means; among all means having determinate ends, tapas is recognized in the world to be the chief (sādhakatamam). Hence, though not specifically taught by the father, Bhṛgu took up tapas as the means of Brahman-knowledge. And that tapas is the integration (samādhāna) of the outer and inner instruments, since Brahman-apprehension proceeds through that gate, as the smṛti says: "The supreme tapas is the one-pointedness of mind and senses; that is greater than all dharmas; that is called the supreme dharma." Having so performed tapas —
T_C03_S02_V01: He realized: 'Food is Brahman.' For verily, from food alone are these beings born; having been born, they live by food; into food they finally enter and merge. Having known this, he again approached his father Varuṇa, saying: 'Sir, teach me Brahman.' He said to him: 'Through tapas seek to know Brahman; tapas is Brahman.' He performed tapas; having performed tapas...
T_C03_S02_V01::block-0:
He understood, that is, came to know, 'Food is Brahman.' Indeed, food is endowed with the characteristics already stated for Brahman. How so? Because 'from food alone verily are these beings born; having been born they live by food; and they pass into food, entering it at the end.' Therefore it is reasonable that food possesses Brahman-nature — this is the import.

Having thus performed tapas and having known food as Brahman through both definition (lakṣaṇa) and reasoned demonstration (upapatti), Bhṛgu nevertheless fell once more into doubt and again approached his father Varuṇa, saying: 'Sir, teach me Brahman.' What then is the cause of his renewed doubt? It is answered: it arises from the perception that food itself is something produced (and hence cannot be the unproduced Brahman).

The repeated instruction concerning tapas is intended to firmly establish that tapas is the foremost means of knowledge. So long as the definition of Brahman has not reached its highest, unsurpassable form, and so long as the desire to know has not ceased, tapas alone is your means; therefore, 'through tapas alone seek to know Brahman' — this is the meaning. The rest is straightforward.
T_C03_S03_V01: He realized: 'Prāṇa (life-breath) is Brahman.' For verily, from prāṇa alone are these beings born; having been born they live by prāṇa; into prāṇa they finally enter and merge. Having known this, he again approached his father Varuṇa, saying: 'Sir, teach me Brahman.' He said to him: 'Through tapas seek to know Brahman; tapas is Brahman.' He performed tapas; having performed tapas...
T_C03_S04_V01: He realized: 'Mind is Brahman.' For verily, from mind alone are these beings born; having been born they live by mind; into mind they finally enter and merge. Having known this, he again approached his father Varuṇa, saying: 'Sir, teach me Brahman.' He said to him: 'Through tapas seek to know Brahman; tapas is Brahman.' He performed tapas; having performed tapas...
T_C03_S05_V01: He realized: 'Vijñāna (intellect/cognition) is Brahman.' For verily, from vijñāna alone are these beings born; having been born they live by vijñāna; into vijñāna they finally enter and merge. Having known this, he again approached his father Varuṇa, saying: 'Sir, teach me Brahman.' He said to him: 'Through tapas seek to know Brahman; tapas is Brahman.' He performed tapas; having performed tapas...
T_C03_S06_V01: He realized: 'Ānanda (bliss) is Brahman.' For verily, from ānanda alone are these beings born; having been born they live by ānanda; into ānanda they finally enter and merge. This is the knowledge of Bhṛgu and Varuṇa, established in the supreme firmament (the cave of the heart). Whoever knows thus becomes firmly established; he becomes possessed of food, an eater of food, and grows great — through offspring, cattle, and the radiance of Brahman-knowledge — great in fame.
T_C03_S06_V01::block-0:
Thus, with his self purified by tapas, having failed to find the full mark of Brahman in prāṇa and the others, Bhṛgu, gradually entering inward, came to know the innermost ānanda as Brahman, and that too with tapas as the very means. Therefore, by one who desires to know Brahman, the supreme tapas — namely the concentration of the outer and inner instruments (the senses and the mind) — must be undertaken as the means: this is the purport of the section.

Now, having concluded the narrative, the śruti in its own voice declares the truth that the narrative was meant to convey. 'This is that knowledge of Bhāṛgava' — known by Bhṛgu and taught by Varuṇa, the Vāruṇī Vidyā — 'established in the supreme firmament,' that is, in the cave-space of the heart, in the supreme non-dual ānanda; complete in itself, having proceeded inwardly from the food-self upward.

Whoever else, by the same means of tapas and by this same gradual inward entry, knows ānanda-Brahman — he, by abiding firm in this knowledge, becomes established in the supreme Brahman that is bliss; he becomes Brahman itself — that is the meaning. The visible fruit too is declared: 'annavān' — one in whom abundant food exists; for if it merely meant that food exists for him in some general way, then everyone would be 'annavān' and the special result of the knowledge would be lost.

Likewise 'annāda' — eater of food — that is, one whose digestive fire is bright. He becomes great. By what does this greatness arise? It is said: through offspring (sons and the rest), through cattle (cows, horses and the like), and through brahma-varcas — the splendour born of self-control, sense-restraint, knowledge, and the rest. He becomes great in fame, that is, in the renown that springs from noble conduct.
T_C03_S07_V01: Let one not despise food: that is the vow. Prāṇa indeed is food; the body is the eater of food. In prāṇa the body is established; in the body prāṇa is established. Thus this food is established in food. Whoever knows this food established in food becomes firmly established; he becomes possessed of food, an eater of food, and grows great — through offspring, cattle, and the radiance of Brahman-knowledge — great in fame.
T_C03_S07_V01::block-0:
Further: since Brahman was known with food itself serving as the doorway, therefore food, like a teacher, must not be despised. This is enjoined as the vow of the one who has known Brahman in this manner. The injunction of this vow serves to extol food, and food deserves such praise because it has been the means of attaining Brahman.

'Prāṇa is indeed food' — because prāṇa is contained within the body. Whatever is established within another, that is food in relation to it. The body is established in prāṇa, hence prāṇa is food and the body is the eater. Likewise the body too is food and prāṇa is the eater. How is the body established in prāṇa? Because prāṇa is the cause of the body's continued existence.

Therefore both these — body and prāṇa — are at once food and eater. By that whereby each is established in the other, each is food; by that whereby each gives a base to the other, each is eater. Hence prāṇa and the body, both, are food and eater alike.

Whoever thus knows this food established in food becomes firmly established — established in the very nature of food and eater. Further, 'he becomes possessed of food, an eater of food,' and so on, as before.
T_C03_S08_V01: Let one not reject food: that is the vow. The waters indeed are food; light (fire) is the eater of food. In the waters light is established; in light the waters are established. Thus this food is established in food. Whoever knows this food established in food becomes firmly established; he becomes possessed of food, an eater of food, and grows great — through offspring, cattle, and the radiance of Brahman-knowledge — great in fame.
T_C03_S08_V01::block-0:
'Let one not reject food' — let one not cast it aside. This is the vow, having the same purpose of praise as before. Food, being thus not discarded by reckoning some kinds as auspicious and others as inauspicious, becomes praised and made great.

In the same manner, what has just been said is to be applied also to the subsequent passages such as 'The waters verily are food,' and so on.
T_C03_S09_V01: Let one make food abundant: that is the vow. The earth indeed is food; the ākāśa (space) is the eater of food. In the earth ākāśa is established; in ākāśa the earth is established. Thus this food is established in food. Whoever knows this food established in food becomes firmly established; he becomes possessed of food, an eater of food, and grows great — through offspring, cattle, and the radiance of Brahman-knowledge — great in fame.
T_C03_S09_V01::block-0: For one who meditates upon waters and light as having the qualities of food and eater (as taught in 'in the waters light is established'), the vow is to make food abundant.
T_C03_S10_V01: Let one not turn anyone away from one’s dwelling — that is the vow. Therefore, by whatever means possible, one should procure abundant food. ‘Food has been made ready for him,’ they declare. To one who in the foremost manner gives food, food is made ready in the foremost manner. To one who in a middling manner gives food, food is made ready in a middling manner. To one who in the lowest manner gives food, food is made ready in the lowest manner.
T_C03_S10_V01::block-0:
Likewise, the one who meditates on earth and ākāśa should not turn away anyone — ‘kañcana’ means even a single person — who comes seeking shelter; that is, one should not refuse a guest who has come for lodging. And once shelter has been granted, food too must necessarily be given. Hence, ‘by whatever means possible’ — by any procedure whatsoever — ‘one should procure abundant food’; this means: one should make a great store of food. Since the wise who possess food say to a guest, to one who has come desiring food, ‘arādhi’ — ‘it has been made ready, food has been prepared for him’ — and they do not refuse him by saying ‘there is none,’ for that very reason one should procure abundant food: this is the connection with what precedes.

Further, the greatness of the gift of food is now declared: in whatever manner one gives food, in just that very manner does food return and present itself. How? This is what the text says: ‘etadvai mukhato’nnaṁ rāddham’ — this food is given ‘mukhataḥ,’ that is, in the foremost stage of life, or by the foremost mode of conduct, with worship and reverence preceding the gift, to a guest who seeks food; the words ‘he gives’ are to be supplied as the completion of the sentence. And what fruit accrues to him? It is said: ‘mukhato’smā annaṁ rādhyate’ — ‘mukhataḥ,’ in the earliest stage of life, or by the foremost mode, food is made ready for him who has given food; meaning, just as he has given, so it returns and serves him. So too ‘madhyataḥ’ — in the middle stage of life and by middling treatment; and likewise ‘antataḥ’ — in the last stage of life, by the lowest mode of treatment, with disrespect — in that very manner does food come about and present itself to him.
T_C03_S10_V02: He who knows thus. Brahman is to be meditated upon as ‘kṣema’ in speech; as ‘yogakṣema’ in the prāṇa and apāna; as ‘karman’ in the hands; as ‘gati’ in the feet; as ‘vimukti’ in the anus. These are the human cognitions. Now the divine. ‘Tṛpti’ in rain; ‘bala’ in lightning.
T_C03_S10_V02::block-0:
‘He who knows thus’ — he who knows the aforesaid greatness of food and the fruit of giving it, to him the stated fruit accrues. Now the mode of meditation upon Brahman is taught: ‘kṣema iti vāci’ — ‘kṣema’ means the preservation of what has already been acquired. Brahman is established in speech in the form of kṣema — thus is it to be meditated upon.

‘Yogakṣema iti’ — ‘yoga’ is the acquisition of what has not yet been acquired. Although these two — yoga and kṣema — arise when prāṇa and apāna are vigorous, even so they are not caused by prāṇa and apāna alone; rather they are caused by Brahman. Therefore Brahman, in the form of yoga-kṣema, stands established in prāṇa and apāna — thus it is to be meditated upon. In the same way, in the others that follow, by that and that respective form, Brahman alone is to be meditated upon.

Since action is accomplished by Brahman, in the hands Brahman established in the form of action is to be meditated upon. ‘Gati’ in the feet; ‘vimukti’ in the anus. These are the ‘mānuṣyaḥ samājñāḥ’ — cognitions occurring in human beings; that is, the inner cognitions, kinds of knowledge, and meditations pertaining to the body — this is the meaning. Now ‘daivīḥ’ — divine cognitions, those occurring among the gods, are stated. ‘Tṛpti iti vṛṣṭau’ — since rain, by the channel of food and the rest, is the cause of satisfaction, Brahman alone, in the form of satisfaction, stands established in rain — thus to be meditated upon; and likewise in the others, by their respective forms, Brahman alone is to be meditated upon. So too in lightning, in the form of strength.
T_C03_S10_V03: ‘Yaśas’ in cattle; ‘jyotis’ in the stars; ‘prajāti, amṛta, ānanda’ in the generative organ; ‘sarvam’ in ākāśa. One should meditate upon Him as ‘pratiṣṭhā’ — one becomes possessed of foundation. One should meditate upon Him as ‘mahas’ — one becomes great. One should meditate upon Him as ‘manas’ — one becomes endowed with reflection.
T_C03_S10_V03::block-0: In cattle, in the form of glory; in the stars, in the form of light. ‘Prajāti’ — progeny; ‘amṛta’ — the attainment of immortality through a son, by way of release from the debts; ‘ānanda’ — happiness: all this, having the generative organ as its instrument, is Brahman alone established in the generative organ in this form, and is so to be meditated upon. Everything indeed is established in ākāśa; therefore whatever ‘all’ there is, established in ākāśa, that is Brahman alone — so it is to be meditated upon; and that ākāśa is itself Brahman. Hence one should meditate upon Him as the foundation of all. By meditating on the quality of being the foundation, one becomes ‘pratiṣṭhāvān’ — possessed of foundation. So in all the others. Whatever fruit is here described, that is Brahman alone; by meditating on it, one becomes possessed of it — thus is it to be understood; and from another śruti also: ‘In whatever way they meditate upon Him, that very thing one becomes’ (cf. Chā. Up. 3.14.1). ‘Tanmaha ityupāsīta’ — one should meditate upon Him as endowed with the quality of greatness. One becomes great. ‘Tanmana ityupāsīta’ — manas is reflection. One becomes ‘mānavān’ — competent in reflection.
T_C03_S10_V04: One should meditate upon Him as ‘nama’ — desired objects bow down to him. One should meditate upon Him as ‘Brahman’ — one becomes possessed of Brahman. One should meditate upon Him as ‘the surrounding-death of Brahman’ — around him die his hating rivals; around him die his unloving co-heirs. He who is here in man and He who is yonder in the sun — He is one.
T_C03_S10_V04::block-0: ‘Tannama ityupāsīta’ — bowing down is ‘namas’; one should meditate upon Him as endowed with the quality of bowing-down. ‘Namyante asmai kāmāḥ’ — desired things bow down, become submissive, to this meditator; ‘kāmāḥ’ are objects that are sought after, namely the enjoyable sense-objects. ‘Tad brahmetyupāsīta’ — one should meditate upon Him as Brahman, that is, as the most expansive. One becomes ‘brahmavān’ — possessed of that quality. ‘Tad brahmaṇaḥ parimara ityupāsīta’ — the ‘parimara of Brahman’ means: around it die the five deities — lightning, rain, moon, sun, fire. Hence Vāyu is the parimara, as is well-known from another śruti. That very Vāyu is non-different from ākāśa; thus ākāśa is the parimara of Brahman. Therefore ākāśa, having Vāyu for its essence, is the parimara of Brahman — so it is to be meditated upon. ‘Enam’ — him, the knower thus, his rival haters; even those who do not hate, since they too become co-heirs (sapatnāḥ), are qualified by ‘the haters who are co-heirs.’ These haters who are co-heirs ‘pari-mriyante’ — die around him, give up their breaths. Furthermore, the unloving brātṛvyas, even though not haters, also die around him.
T_C03_S10_V04::block-1: Beginning with ‘prāṇo vā annaṁ śarīramannādam’ down to ‘ākāśa’ as the last, the relation of being food and food-eater has been declared of the effect alone. — But what is the use of saying so? — By it this is established: that the saṁsāra characterized by enjoyer-and-enjoyed pertains only to the realm of effects, not to the Self. In the Self, however, it is figuratively predicated through delusion. — But the individual self too is an effect of the supreme Self; hence saṁsāra is fitting for it. — No, because the śruti speaks of the entrance of one who is non-saṁsāric: ‘Having created it, into that itself He entered’ (Tai. Up. 2.6.1) — for it is precisely the supreme Self, the cause of ākāśa and the rest, who is non-saṁsāric, whose entrance into the effects is heard of. Therefore the jīva-ātman who has entered into the effect is none other than the supreme, the non-saṁsāric one — and this is also justified by the cogency of a single agent for ‘having created’ and ‘He entered.’ For if it is one agent who performs both creation and entrance, then the suffix ‘ktvā’ (in sṛṣṭvā) is appropriate. — But the śruti might mean that one who has entered has assumed a different mode of being. — No; for the entrance has been refuted as having a different purport. — But by the special śruti ‘by this jīva-ātman’ (Chā. Up. 6.3.2), entrance is by way of a distinct attribute. — No; because identity is again declared by ‘that thou art’ (Chā. Up. 6.8.16). — But the upāsanā as identity is meant to remove the assumption of separate being for one who has assumed a different state. — No; because of the co-referentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) in ‘that is the truth,’ ‘that is the Self,’ ‘that thou art’ (Chā. Up. 6.8.16). — But the saṁsāric character of the jīva is directly observed. — No; because the perceiver cannot itself be the perceived. — But the Self qualified by the dharmas of saṁsāra is observed. — No; because the dharmas are not other than the dharmin, and so the relation of object-of-action does not hold — just as in the case of heat and light, burnability and being-illumined cannot apply. — But from witnessing fear and the like, sorrow and the rest are inferred (in the Self). — No; because fear and sorrow are themselves objects of perception, and what is perceived cannot be a property of the perceiver. — But this contradicts the reasoning-systems of Kapila, Kaṇāda and the rest. — No; for they are devoid of foundation, and being in conflict with the Veda, their being deluded is established. Thus from śruti and from reason it is established that the Self is non-saṁsāric and is one. — How is its oneness shown? — It is said: ‘He who is here in man and He who is yonder in the sun — He is one,’ and so on, all to be construed as before.
T_C03_S10_V05: He who knows thus, departing from this world, ascending to this Self made of food, ascending to this Self made of prāṇa, ascending to this Self made of mind, ascending to this Self made of vijñāna, ascending to this Self made of bliss, roaming through these worlds, eating what he wishes and assuming what form he wishes, sits singing this sāman: ‘Hā-vu, hā-vu, hā-vu!’
T_C03_S10_V05::block-0:
Having ascended through the order beginning with the food-made and ending with the bliss-made Self, he sits singing this sāman. The meaning of the verse ‘satyaṁ jñānam’ has already been expounded at length by the Ānanda-vallī, which is its commentary. But the import of the fruit-statement, ‘he obtains all desires together with Brahman the wise’ (Tai. Up. 2.1.1), has not yet been amplified. What are those desires? Of what range are ‘all desires’? And how does he obtain them together with Brahman? — All this is now to be expounded; therefore this section is begun.

There, in the father-and-son narrative which forms the supplement to the prior knowledge, austerity has been declared as the means to brahma-vidyā. The relation of food and food-eater has also been laid down for the effect — from prāṇa down to ākāśa — and meditations regarding Brahman have been taught. And those manifold desires, accomplished by their respective specific means and resting upon the various effects beginning with ākāśa, have been displayed. But in oneness, the position of being a desirer of desires becomes untenable, since the entire host of distinctions has become the very Self. There, how does the knower-thus simultaneously, in the form of Brahman, obtain all desires? — It is said: because of the cogency of being the Self of all. How is sarvātmatva established? — It is replied: by the knowledge of the oneness of the Self abiding in puruṣa and in the sun, casting aside what is high and low, ascending in order through the food-made and the rest — selves fashioned by avidyā — up to the ānandamaya, and having reached the truth-knowledge-infinite Brahman, characterized by qualities such as adṛśya and the rest, naturally blissful, unborn, immortal, fearless, non-dual, as the very fruit, he passes through these worlds beginning with bhūr — the connection being made across the intervening words. How does he pass through? ‘Kāmānnī’ — he whose food is according to his wish; likewise ‘kāmarūpī’ — he whose forms are according to his wish; passing through, as the Self of all, experiencing these worlds as his own Self. What does he do? ‘He sits singing this sāman.’ Because of equality (samatva), Brahman itself is the sāman; as one whose form is non-distinct from all, he sings — that is, sounds forth — proclaiming the oneness of the Self for the benefit of the worlds, and singing his utter fulfillment, the fruit of that knowledge, he sits. How? ‘Hā-vu, hā-vu, hā-vu’ — this is in the sense of ‘aho!’, employed to convey extreme wonder.
T_C03_S10_V06: ‘I am food, I am food, I am food. I am the food-eater, I am the food-eater, I am the food-eater. I am the maker of the verse, I am the maker of the verse, I am the maker of the verse. I am the first-born of the cosmic order. Before the gods I am at the navel of immortality. He who gives Me, he indeed thus saves Me. I, the food, eat the eater of food. I have overcome this whole world. My light is like the sun.’ He who knows thus. Such is the upaniṣad.
T_C03_S10_V06::block-0: What, then, is that wonder? — It is said:
T_C03_S10_V06::block-1:
The non-dual Self, though wholly untainted, is itself I — the food and the food-eater. Moreover, I alone am the maker of the verse. ‘Śloka’ means the conjunction of food and food-eater; its maker is the conscious one. Or else, the maker of the conjunction — that is, the one who, for the sake of food, which exists for the sake of another (the eater), brings together what is of many kinds, by reason of its existing for another’s purpose. The threefold repetition is to convey wonder. ‘I am, I become.’ ‘Prathamajāḥ’ means prathamaja — first-born, the foremost to arise. ‘Ṛtasya’ — of truth, of this universe, gross and subtle; before the gods I am the ‘nābhi of immortality’ — the navel of immortality, the middle, that immortality of beings which abides in Me — such is the meaning. Whoever gives Me, the food, to those who seek food — speaks of Me as food — ‘sa it’: he indeed, in just this manner, preserves Me, undestroyed, exactly as I am: ‘āvāḥ’ means he saves. But he who, on the other hand, without giving Me to seekers when the time has come, eats food himself — that man, eating food, I, being the food, presently eat in turn; that is, I devour him.

Here it is objected: in that case I am afraid of liberation, which is the attainment of being the Self of all; let saṁsāra alone remain, lest, even when liberated, I, having become food, should be eaten by another. Be not afraid: for the eating of all desires belongs to the sphere of empirical usage; and this knower, having transcended the empirical sphere — characterized by food, food-eater, etc., fashioned by avidyā — has by vidyā attained the state of Brahman. For him no second thing exists, of which he could be afraid. Hence one ought not to fear liberation. Then what is meant by ‘I am food, I am the food-eater’? It is said: this empirical usage of food, food-eater, and the rest — being effect-bound — is mere empirical usage; it is not the supreme reality. Yet, even being thus, since it is caused by Brahman and apart from Brahman is non-existent, it is uttered for the praise of brahma-bhāva, the fruit of brahma-vidyā: ‘I am food, I am food, I am food. I am the food-eater, I am the food-eater, I am the food-eater,’ and so on. Hence even the slightest taint of the defect of fear, caused by avidyā, does not exist for one who, by the cessation of avidyā, has become Brahman. ‘I have overcome the entire world (bhuvana)’ — the world (bhuvana), so called because it is to be enjoyed (sambhajanīya) by beings, or because beings come to be (bhavanti) in it, or because beings come to be from it through Brahmā and the rest; this whole I have overcome — I overpower — by the supreme Lord-form which is My own nature. ‘Suvarna jyotīḥ’ — ‘suvar’ is the sun; the ‘na’ is in the sense of comparison; like the sun, ever-shining and undimmed, is My light, that is, My radiance. Such is the upaniṣad — the knowledge of the supreme Self — laid down by the two vallīs; this very upaniṣad, as declared, having become tranquil, controlled, withdrawn, forbearing, and concentrated, having undertaken great austerity like Bhṛgu, whoever knows thus — for him there is this fruit, namely the liberation already declared.
